entries.title: Blackhawks' Kevin Korchinski hopes to 'prove I belong' in back-against-wall season
entries.summary: <p>The last three years have been a rocky road for defenseman <b>Kevin Korchinski</b>,<b> Kyle Davidson’s</b> first draft pick as the Blackhawks’ general manager in 2022.</p><p>It hasn’t been all bad, but things haven’t gone exactly the way Korchinski or the Hawks would have hoped since he turned pro.</p><p>Korchinski, 22, now enters his fourth pro season in a make-or-break situation. He’s no longer exempt from waivers, which basically locks him into an NHL roster spot — at least for now — because the Hawks won’t risk losing a top-10 selection that easily.</p><p>But playing time is far from guaranteed. Davidson has said he’s more comfortable than ever with young players sitting out as healthy scratches now that the Hawks are prioritizing trying to win every night.</p><p>Coach <b>Jeff Blashill</b> has said Korchinski appears more confident and his skating ‘‘more controlled.’’ But he also admitted Sunday that Korchinski isn’t one of the Hawks’ top six defensemen right now.</p><p>Korchinski looked like arguably the best player on the ice in the Hawks’ first preseason matchup with the Wild on Saturday, when the teams predominantly dressed AHL rosters. But he wasn’t part of the largely NHL lineup that earned a 4-3 overtime victory in the rematch Monday.</p><p>Korchinski will have to earn every regular-season game and minute, and he understands that.</p><p>‘‘[My goal is to] prove I belong here and that I want to be part of this culture,’’ he said.</p><p>Korchinksi has been limited in the past by his subpar strength against NHL competition. He couldn’t, for example, consistently box out opponents around his net. That’s part of why the Hawks have been outscored 95-52 in his 105 NHL games to date.</p><p>He hopes he has addressed that weakness. He’s now 198 pounds, up 10 from the end of last season but roughly the same as he was last September. But not all changes are reflected in weight.</p><p>‘‘I definitely got stronger and my gym numbers got better,’’ Korchinski said. ‘‘My approach, rather than gaining a lot of weight, [was] more trying to get stronger.’’</p><h3>Preseason victory</h3><p>A victory was expected Monday, considering the Hawks dressed a far superior lineup than the Wild. <b>Bowen Byram </b>eventually gave them that by completing a hat trick in his unofficial first appearance at the United Center with the Hawks.</p><p><b>Patrick Kane</b> didn’t play, but Byram, <b>Nick Lardis</b> and <b>Roman Kantserov </b>were standouts.</p><p>Blashill liked how the Hawks held on to pucks longer in the offensive zone, but he noted they gave up too many odd-man rushes and showed signs of fatigue after five consecutive grueling days of training camp.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" > <div class="TweetUrl"> <blockquote class="twitter-tweet"><p lang="en" dir="ltr">Bowen Byram OT WINNER FOR THE HAT TRICK! <a href="https://t.co/ez9IihRNAC">pic.twitter.com/ez9IihRNAC</a></p>— BHF (@BlackhawksFocus) <a href="https://x.com/BlackhawksFocus/status/2102223892496757214?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">September 22, 2026</a></blockquote> <script async src="https://platform.x.com/widgets.js" charset="utf-8"></script> </div> </div> </div></div><p></p><h3><b>Commesso belongs</b></h3><p>Goalie prospect <b>Drew Commesso</b> also gained some weight during the summer, adding six pounds to get up to 190.</p><p>‘‘The biggest area I feel it in is my legs,’’ Commesso said. ‘‘My leg strength around the posts, I did a ton of work on that this summer. Comparing video from last year, I definitely see a difference. The NHL is really fast, so if I can improve just a millisecond, it’s going to lead to more saves.’’</p><p>After earning his first two NHL victories and first shutout last season, the 24-year-old now sees himself as an NHL-caliber goalie.</p><p>‘‘I belong at that level, and [I have] the mindset that I’m there,’’ he said. ‘‘That allows me to carry myself a little differently in a lot of good ways.’’</p><p>Commesso won’t start this season at the NHL level, but opportunities should come his way during the season. With a new two-year contract in hand, he could take over as the Hawks’ full-time backup by next season.</p>
entries.author: Ben Pope

entries.title: Chicago police fatally shoot dog that attacked them in Humboldt Park
entries.summary: <p>Chicago police shot and killed a dog that attacked them while the officers were working on an investigation in the Humboldt Park neighborhood Monday, police said.</p><p>Shortly before 5 p.m., the officers were in the 700 block of North Christiana Avenue when a dog approached and attacked an officer. One of the officers then shot the dog. </p><p>The dog died and the city's Department of Animal Care and Control was notified.</p><p>Three officers were taken to nearby hospitals in good condition. No other injuries were reported.</p><p>Detectives are continuing to investigate the incident.</p>
entries.author: Sun-Times Wire

entries.title: For Blackhawks, Jordan Greenway's defensive acumen makes him sneaky-smart addition
entries.summary: <p>While the hockey world erupted into furious debate over the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/blackhawks" target="_blank" >Blackhawks</a>’ blockbuster trade for defenseman Bowen Byram in June, one piece flew under the radar.</p><p>Veteran forward Jordan Greenway quietly came to Chicago in the deal. Although his inclusion might have been a salary dump on the Sabres’ end — his $4 million salary-cap hit was outsized for his role in their lineup — it was welcomed on the Hawks’ end.</p><p>‘‘Jordan brings a heaviness, a physicality to our group that we could use,’’ general manager Kyle Davidson said afterward. ‘‘He’s a really big body that can get in on the forecheck and make life difficult for opposing -defenders.’’</p><p>The Hawks enter this season with two scrappy forwards — Greenway and Andrew Mangiapane — whom contenders were eager to dump last spring but whom they consider to be worthwhile buy-low experiments.</p><p>It appears both will have spots in the opening-night lineup. Mangiapane has skated on the third line with <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/blackhawks/2026/09/20/blackhawks-oliver-moore-nick-lardis-depth-roles-training" target="_blank" >Oliver Moore</a> and Ryan Donato so far.</p><p>Greenway has skated on the fourth — alongside Ryan Greene and free-agent signing Cole Smith — while playing on the penalty kill, as well.</p><p>The Hawks are optimistic about the potential impact on the fourth line, aside from the nickname confusion with two guys called ‘‘Greener’’ skating side-by-side.</p><p>‘‘It’s a line I would feel very comfortable putting out against anybody,’’ coach Jeff Blashill said.</p><p>You also could say it’s an eco-friendly line. Greenway apparently suggested an alternative nickname — a surely not-work-appropriate one — that Blashill refuses to use.</p><p>It’s possible Greenway will end up being the Pat Maroon of this Hawks team. Like Maroon, he’s massive (6-6 and 231 pounds), sometimes silly off the ice and sometimes mean on it.</p><p>But it’s also possible Greenway, unlike Maroon, will end up becoming a significant depth contributor for these Hawks.</p><p>‘‘I don’t know if it’s unfortunately or fortunately, but I think I’m a little bit older on this team, which is kind of nuts,’’ Greenway said Monday. ‘‘[I’m] just trying to lead these guys, bring some confidence to the squad. On the ice, I’ll continue to do as I do: play a power forward-type game, create some space and bring a physical presence.’’</p><p>There was a time during the first chapter of Greenway’s career with the Wild when he formed one-third of one of the most effective shutdown lines in the NHL.</p><p>In 2021 and 2022, the Wild trio of Greenway, Joel Eriksson Ek and Marcus Foligno regularly faced opponents’ best players and dominated them. In 749 minutes together across two seasons, that line outscored opponents 45-16 with a 57.6% scoring-chance ratio.</p><p>‘‘I’ve been doing it my whole career,’’ Greenway said. ‘‘I enjoy playing against the top lines, trying to shut them down and frustrate them.’’</p><p>He was similarly effective in 2023-24 with the Sabres, too, albeit without such consistent linemates. He chipped in 28 points and racked up 141 hits.</p><p>Analytics models rated him as one of the best defensive forwards in the league that season, which is worth noting, even though Blashill recently made the case NHL analytics haven’t yet figured out how to evaluate defensive play accurately.</p><p>Greenway wasn’t able to maintain that momentum the last two seasons, though. Hernia problems limited him to 74 games, during which his production and ice time declined and his analytics worsened.</p><p>He is healthy now, and he’s still in his 20s until February. He’s excited about this new opportunity in Chicago afforded to him by the trade, even if the debate it stirred up didn’t involve him.</p><p>‘‘It’s a great group here,’’ he said. ‘‘You can see how motivated the guys are. They’re trying to make a name for themselves and really do some good things. If we can all start off strong from the get-go, if we can find [out] what we need to do early, we’ll be good.’’</p>

entries.title: Man suspected of fatally slicing woman's neck in Englewood taken into custody
entries.summary: <p>A man who apparently plunged a knife into the neck of a woman, killing her, has been arrested and was in critical condition at a hospital after the early Tuesday attack in Englewood. </p><p>The woman was found lying on the ground with a stab wound to her neck in the 7300 block of South Emerald Avenue around 1:40 a.m., Chicago police said. </p><p>The unidentified woman was taken to the University of Chicago Medical Center where she was pronounced dead, police said. </p><p>Officers who were searching the early discovered the apparent attacker, a man who was found on a nearby porch with a cut to his right hand, police said. </p><p>He was also taken to the University of Chicago Medical Center in critical condition and was placed under arrest, according to police, who said the knife used to kill the woman was recovered. </p><p>Area 1 detectives were investigating and no charges have been announced.</p>

entries.title: Dear Abby: I attend friends' events, but many skipped my mother's memorial
entries.summary: <p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> My mom died of extreme old age recently. She was a sweet woman everyone loved. I sent invitations to her memorial, and I'm getting a lot of excuses for why my friends can't attend. I am upset.</p><p>In my circle of friends (all similar ages), I was the last to graduate, get a career job, start a relationship, buy a house, be married and so forth. I've attended my friends' graduations, weddings, baby showers, milestone birthdays, and family funerals, yet there hasn't been much reciprocation.</p><p>Excuses for not attending Mom's memorial included going to a grandkid's soccer game and attending a 2-year-old's birthday party. Really? I know I'm dealing with unusually strong emotions due to Mom's death, but I want to scream, "This is MY MOM," not some distant friend or relative. My spouse says I shouldn't stress and that all we need is each other (said by someone who has a huge, loving family whereas my family is just me and my dad). How do I deal with my feelings of resentment, abandonment and being a low priority? — <i>LAST ONE IN CALIFORNIA</i></p><p><b>DEAR LAST ONE:</b> Your spouse is right. In the final analysis, all you need is each other — though a few supportive friends would certainly be welcome. I have always said that funerals are for the living, not the deceased. Be grateful for the support you are receiving from the people who accepted the invitation to your mother's funeral. They are your core support group; the others are mere acquaintances, so start thinking of them in those terms.</p><p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> I rent a two-bedroom apartment, which I shared with my best friend. When he moved away last month due to a work relocation, I advertised the room, and a couple moved in. They are friendly and pay their rent on time, but their cooking produces extremely strong smells that I cannot tolerate. My medication causes hypersensitivity to odors, and I can no longer stand to be in the kitchen because the smells linger. They also live on a very different schedule from me. As a result, my diet and sleep are both suffering. They remain unaware of how the adjustment has affected me because I don't feel they are doing anything wrong.</p><p>I would like to move out into a studio of my own. The lease on this apartment is currently a month-to-month, so the only thing keeping me here is the guilt I feel about burdening my roommates with this. They will have to move out, find a replacement for me or take on the full rent themselves. I want to do right by them, but I know it would be best for me to leave. What is the proper course of action here? — <i>DOOMED IN AUSTRALIA</i></p><p><b>DEAR DOOMED:</b> There is no reason why you should feel guilty for leveling with this couple; your health must come first. Explain the problem to them and tell them that while you like them personally, your health is being affected by the cooking odors. Tell them that because you are now on a month-to-month lease, you plan to move to a smaller place of your own and give them the option of staying or moving. Consider this a first step in learning to stand up for yourself.</p><p><i>Dear Abby is written by Abigail Van Buren. For nearly four decades, Jeanne Phillips penned this column, which was founded in 1956 by her mother, Pauline Phillips. Contact Dear Abby at www.DearAbby.com or P.O. Box 270135, Kansas City, MO 64127.</i></p>

entries.title: Book profiles Gay sisters, an overlooked Chicago gospel trio who played with Mahalia Jackson, Sam Cooke
entries.summary: <p>If you name any gospel music star of the mid-20th century, Gregory Donald Gay probably has a story about them.</p><p>His family was visited by singer Clara Ward, who would pull her 1957 Chrysler limousine into the driveway of their Woodlawn home.</p><p>As a starstruck teenager, he sang before the “father of gospel music,” Thomas A. Dorsey.</p><p>At 5 years old, he witnessed icon Mahalia Jackson having a fit<b> </b>backstage at Carnegie Hall after Ward’s group – particularly Marion Williams<b> –</b> brought the house down.</p><p>“She didn't want anybody to outsing her,” said Gay, now 81 and the longtime pastor of the Prayer Center Church of God in Christ in Woodlawn.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Gregory Donald Gay, 81, is the longtime pastor of the Prayer Center Church of God in Christ in Woodlawn. He co-wrote a new book, “Can I Get a Witness! Faith, Family and Chicago Gospel Music,” about his sisters’ influential singing group. </p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Candace Dane Chambers/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>As the younger brother of the Gay Sisters gospel group, he had a front row seat for the action<b> </b>during gospel’s golden age. Now, he is sharing his tales in a recently released book, “Can I Get a Witness! Faith, Family and Chicago Gospel Music” (The University of Chicago Press). The text was co-written with Steven B. Dolins, 69-year-old founder and president of The Sirens Records music label in Highland Park.</p><p>Gay said his sisters would have been forgotten without Dolins.</p><p>“I'm grateful for him opening up a window and letting the general public look in,” Gay said. “They were great, talented people, but I don't think they got a fair break.”</p><p>Gay’s late siblings — Evelyn, Geraldine and Mildred — performed, recorded or rubbed elbows with Ward, Jackson, Sam Cooke, the Staple Singers, James Cleveland, Sister Rosetta Tharpe, Dizzy Gillespie and Sonny Rollins. They released music on the legendary Savoy, Decca and Chess labels; toured the country and helped bring gospel to a televised audience. Their 1951 hit record, “God Will Take Care of You,” was later covered by Aretha Franklin.</p><p>But their accomplishments have been overlooked, and their records are difficult to find beyond streaming sites or YouTube.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-fc0000" name="image-fc0000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/439cef1/2147483647/strip/true/crop/8192x4598+0+433/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F87%2Ff8%2F189e82ad4e9b8407d1b22f9c0f7d%2Fgospelbook-260907-018.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/012bc3b/2147483647/strip/true/crop/8192x4598+0+433/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F87%2Ff8%2F189e82ad4e9b8407d1b22f9c0f7d%2Fgospelbook-260907-018.jpg 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/6149c15/2147483647/strip/true/crop/8192x4598+0+433/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F87%2Ff8%2F189e82ad4e9b8407d1b22f9c0f7d%2Fgospelbook-260907-018.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="Copies of Steven B. Faith, Family and Chicago Gospel Music,” lie on a table at Prayer Center Church of God In Christ in Woodlawn on the South Side.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Candace Dane Chambers/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>The sisters faced both racism and sexism in the music industry. At times, they were not paid or properly credited for their work. Their career was also impacted by personal problems. “Can I Get a Witness!” details their setbacks and triumphs, while recounting music history in Chicago, where scholars say modern gospel music was born.</p><p>Dolins said he was inspired to write the book after recording CDs featuring both Geraldine Gay, who died in 2010, and Gregory Donald Gay, who would regale him with stories. Week after week, Dolins documented Gay’s accounts over lunch – bagels and lox from Once Upon a Bagel in Highland Park – at the pastor’s church.</p><p>“These stories became hallowed ground for me,” said Dolins, also a computer scientist and professor at Bradley University. “It just brought to life his sisters and his mom.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-ca0000" name="image-ca0000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/8e8b350/2147483647/strip/true/crop/7845x4403+0+415/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fbc%2F13%2Fc34cac094055bd4b8654085176f3%2Fgospelbook-260907-004.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/a5d4e11/2147483647/strip/true/crop/7845x4403+0+415/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fbc%2F13%2Fc34cac094055bd4b8654085176f3%2Fgospelbook-260907-004.jpg 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/d05c966/2147483647/strip/true/crop/7845x4403+0+415/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fbc%2F13%2Fc34cac094055bd4b8654085176f3%2Fgospelbook-260907-004.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="Steven B. They often came to her house for a home-cooked meal and prayer. Saxophonist Sonny Rollins, who wrote the book’s foreword before his death this year, even lived with the Gay family following his stint at a drug rehabilitation facility. (Fannie Gay is memorialized with an honorary street sign in front of her son’s church at East 67th Street and South Rhodes Avenue.)</p><p>Fannie Gay also supported the musical talents of her daughters, paying for their music lessons and tagging along on their gigs.<b> </b>After forming in the 1940s, the Gay sisters quickly built a reputation in Chicago and made key connections in the New Evelyn was one of Mahalia Jackson’s first accompanists, and they both mentored gospel star James Cleveland.</p><p>“Evelyn’s style was bluesier,” Gregory Donald Gay said. “She was a songwriter. If she could hear you talk, she knew what key you sang in.<b>”</b></p><p>Geraldine, an aficionado of pianist Erroll Garner, leaned more toward jazz, Gay said.</p><p>“And then there was my middle sister, Mildred, who was a great singer,” he said. “I really think that Mildred could’ve sang with the Metropolitan Opera because she had a tremendous range.”</p><div class="Enhancement" entries.title: School Board candidate defends disciplining his kids, says school staff should never use corporal punishment
entries.summary: <p>Fifteen years ago, in the wake of a contentious divorce, the ex-wife of a candidate currently running to be Chicago’s school board president told a judge she wanted an emergency change of custody after her teenage son came to her with a swollen face and scratches, saying he’d gotten them from his father, Victor Henderson.</p><p>One of Henderson’s opponents has seized on the allegations as evidence that he’s unfit to lead the school board.</p><p>Henderson acknowledges that he disciplined his children, but denies that he ever abused them. He told WBEZ and Chalkbeat in a statement that “the court never suspended my parenting time, it never ordered supervised visits, and it did not restrict my relationship with my children.”</p><p>Immediately after the ex-wife’s allegations, the court ordered the children to stay with their mother. But court records reviewed by WBEZ show that Henderson resumed having overnight, unsupervised parenting time with his children.</p><p>After <a class="Link" href="https://www.nbcchicago.com/news/local/candidate-for-chicago-school-board-president-faced-abuse-allegations-court-records-show/3980275/" target="_blank" ><u>NBC5 first reported the story</u></a> in late August, Jessica Biggs, another candidate for school board president, <a class="Link" href="https://x.com/biggs4chicago/status/2092999558665998473" target="_blank" ><u>wrote on the social media platform X</u></a>: “Someone with a history of domestic violence and corporal punishment should not be in a leadership position, especially not for children.”</p><p>Corporal punishment is legal in Illinois but banned in Illinois schools. To decide if corporal punishment is “excessive,” <a class="Link" href="https://www.isba.org/sections/childlaw/newsletter/2015/04/whendoescorporalpunishmentbecomeexc" target="_blank" ><u>a court would typically consider</u></a> the age of the child, if they were injured and how badly and whether the child experienced any trauma from the discipline.</p><p>In a statement, Henderson drew a distinction between what parents may do to discipline their children and what school staff can do. “Teachers should never use corporal punishment with students,” he said.</p><p>The position of school board president is unpaid, but powerful, as that person controls what makes it on the agenda. Some see this <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/elections/2026/graphics/chicago-school-board-education-voter-guide/school-board/president/" target="_blank" ><u>heated fourway race</u></a> as a proxy for the upcoming mayoral election and an opportunity to seize control of the school board from the Chicago Teachers Union. Right now, a majority of board members are aligned with the CTU. As of Friday, $2.1 million had poured into the race.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Victor Henderson, a prominent attorney, was the first in line to file his paperwork back in May to run for Chicago School Board.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Anthony Vazquez/Sun-Times file</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Henderson, a prominent defense attorney, is self-funding his campaign and has not picked up any endorsements from political groups. But he is supported by U.S. Reps. Danny K. Davis and Robin Kelly and several pastors of big Black churches. He has raised a significant amount of money from individuals, including many lawyers.</p><p>To supporters of Henderson, the only Black candidate, the focus on his ex-wife’s allegations amounts to a “smear campaign” with racist undertones. Hermene Hartman, who is working on Henderson’s campaign, <a class="Link" href="https://ndigo.com/2026/09/02/victor-henderson-the-father-vs-victor-henderson-school-board-president/" target="_blank" ><u>wrote in an opinion piece in N’DIGO</u></a>, the online journal she founded, that the incident “is really about a Black man punishing his son.”</p><p>“We should not turn cultural differences into convenient political weapons,” she wrote. “Bravo, Victor, for raising your sons to be young men with firm discipline.”</p><p>Henderson, in an <a class="Link" href="https://wgntv.com/news/politics/wgn-the-point-politics-chicago-illinois/exclusive-chicago-school-board-president-candidate-responds-to-abuse-allegations/" target="_blank" ><u>interview with WGN’s Tahman Bradley</u></a>, said the criticism shows a lack of cultural understanding.</p><p>“I had to raise my children,” he said, noting he took them to church, school, soccer and basketball games and chess matches. “On a rare occasion, if my children needed to be disciplined because they weren’t adhering to the household rules or even did something that was pretty bad, then, as a father, as an African American father, as a Black father, I had to address it. The alternative was to let my kids run amok, and that wasn’t going to happen.”</p><h3>Henderson kept custody of kids in messy legal battle, records show</h3><p>Henderson says his current relationship with all of his now-adult children is “fantastic” and that they have been involved in his school board campaign. But officials with Henderson’s campaign said the sons did not want to talk about what had been a “painful period” in the family’s history.</p><p>Henderson’s ex-wife, through her attorney, declined to comment.</p><p>The Cook County Circuit Court only has online records from 2012 onward, making it difficult to piece together everything that happened in Henderson’s divorce and custody case.</p><p>Some details are clear: Henderson filed for divorce in 2004 and it was finalized in 2008. Henderson and his wife split custody of their two sons, with the boys alternating weeks at their homes. By 2011, Henderson had remarried.</p><p>In January 2011, Henderson’s ex-wife filed an emergency change of custody petition.</p><p>In the custody petition, which was included in a separate filing from 2012, she alleged that their older son told her that Henderson once repeatedly beat him with the wooden handle of a garden hoe, and smashed his iPhone and iPad. The son said Henderson dropped him off the next day at a homeless shelter and told him to volunteer. When the boy learned he was too young to volunteer, he went to his mother’s office and recounted what happened.</p><p>The ex-wife said in the petition that her son’s face was “inflamed” and she saw scratches and bruises. There’s no indication that she called the police. But she said she called her son’s therapist that day and that her son recounted the same story to the therapist. She said her son also told her and the therapist that Henderson “will sometimes” come into his bedroom at night in a “violent rage” and “whip him with a belt when he is asleep under the covers.”</p><p>The judge’s initial reaction was to handwrite an order keeping the boys temporarily with the mom until a court-appointed legal advocate could offer his opinion at a hearing three days later. The judge also ordered both parents not to use corporal punishment on their children.</p><p>The court-appointed advocate’s report or recommendation is not included in available court documents, but a court filing entered in 2012 makes it clear that the boys resumed staying with Henderson every other week.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Victor Henderson is the sole Black candidate in the race for Chicago School Board president. His supporters say the focus on his ex-wife’s allegations amounts to a “smear campaign” with racist undertones.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Victor Hilitski/For the Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>“It is important that reporting distinguish between allegations made during family court proceedings and the actions ultimately taken by the court,” Henderson said in a statement.</p><p>Stacey Platt, a clinical law professor at Loyola University Chicago and interim director of the Civitas ChildLaw Center and Clinic, reviewed the available court records. She said the incident as reported by the mother seems more serious than what would be considered acceptable corporal punishment under state law.</p><p>Platt says she understands that people might question why the ex-wife didn’t call the police, but she points out parents might be hesitant to do so for financial and other reasons. She also says it is important not to assume the accusation is untrue because it was made in the context of a contentious divorce and custody battle.</p><p>Yet Platt said it is telling that the sons were allowed to resume overnight, unsupervised visits with Henderson. She is familiar with the person, known as a guardian ad litem, who was appointed to represent Henderson’s sons in court and she says he is well-respected.</p><p>“At times, we always are afraid we're going to miss something, but I don't believe for a second that he would have agreed to this young man returning to his father's care if he thought he was going to get hurt,” she said.</p><p>Court records filed by the guardian ad litem in 2012 said that there had been “serious allegations made by each of the parties which have required investigation by the guardian ad litem.” WBEZ contacted the guardian ad litem and he declined to comment.</p><h3>Do allegations make Henderson unfit to be school board president?</h3><p>Whether Henderson’s actions or views on hitting children as a form of discipline is relevant to being Chicago school board president is up for debate.</p><p>“Parents have different views on corporal punishment, and I respect that,” he said in a written statement. “My own children are now adults, so it is no longer an issue for me.”</p><p>Illinois banned corporal punishment in public schools in 1993. <a class="Link" href="https://www.pbs.org/newshour/education/hitting-kids-should-never-be-allowed-illinois-bans-corporal-punishment-in-all-schools" target="_blank" ><u>Two years ago, it became one of the few states</u></a> that also bans the practice in private schools. Fifteen states still explicitly allow it in public schools, <a class="Link" href="https://www.npr.org/2026/08/19/nx-s1-5803505/school-corporal-punishment-policy-tracker" target="_blank" ><u>NPR recently reported</u></a>.</p><p>Henderson said that as board president his responsibility would be to “ensure that CPS policies are followed.”</p><p>But he would also pay attention to whether “allegations are investigated fairly, and that every individual receives due process. My personal experiences reinforced for me the importance of carefully evaluating all facts before reaching conclusions.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" a Chicago Public Schools special education teacher was accused</u></a> of routinely using “harmful, physical and violent corporal punishment” on children with disabilities.</p><p>Marvin Hunter, the pastor of Grace Memorial Church on the West Side, said the issue was “a smear campaign in order to make a distraction.”</p><p>He said he endorsed Henderson because, as a certified accountant and lawyer, he possesses skills the school district needs. He also likes that Henderson supports teaching more trades in schools and has connections with corporations that Henderson plans to ask to invest in district programs.</p><p>Hunter said he thinks that people should be more focused on how Henderson’s sons turned out than on his ex-wife’s allegations in their custody case.</p><p>“The facts are his son has fared well,” he said. “We want every one of our children to become a productive part of American society, and his son has done that.”</p><p>During a <a class="Link" href="https://news.wttw.com/2026/09/15/chicago-school-board-president-forum-wttw-news-town-hall" target="_blank" ><u>televised forum on WTTW</u></a> last week, Henderson said his kids love him and he loves them and revisiting this history is “not enjoyable.”</p><p>“It’s a nasty part of politics here in the city of Chicago that somebody's combing through divorce records from 15 and 20 years ago,” he said. “But if that’s the price that I have to pay to help children all across the city, no matter what ZIP code they live in, no matter what language their parents speak, then that’s what I'll do.”</p><p>Of the three candidates running against Henderson for school board president, only Biggs has seized on the ex-wife’s allegation.</p><p>Biggs, a current school board member, is endorsed by the Service Employees International Union, which represents CPS support staff and is in a bitter feud with the CTU. A cadre of wealthy businesspeople, as well as some former CPS leaders, have donated to her campaign.</p><p>Hilario Dominguez, the candidate backed by the CTU, declined to comment. Sendhil Revuluri said he won’t weigh in on a “family matter.”</p><p>“What matters most to me is that every child is loved, protected, and cared for — by their families and by our schools,” Revuluri said in a statement.</p><p><i>Mila Koumpilova of Chalkbeat Chicago contributed reporting.</i></p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/elections/2026/graphics/chicago-school-board-education-voter-guide/school-board/president/" target="_blank" >2026 Voter Guide: Chicago School Board President</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/education/2026/05/22/meet-the-candidates-for-chicagos-first-ever-elected-school-board-president" >Here’s who’s running for Chicago’s first-ever elected school board president</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/education/2026/09/21/what-you-need-to-know-about-chicagos-historic-school-board-election" >What you need to know about Chicago’s historic school board election</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/education/chicago-school-board/2026/07/16/spending-in-chicago-school-board-election-exceeds-1-6-million-as-limits-lift-in-race-for-board-president" >Spending in Chicago school board election exceeds $1.8 million as limits lift in race for board president</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p></p>

entries.title: Everything you need to know about Chicago’s despised parking meters deal
entries.summary: <p>The City Council is facing a Sept. 30 deadline to either approve New York investment firm Stonepeak Partners' $2.53 billion bid to acquire Chicago parking meters, or roll the dice in arbitration and in court.</p><p>Before casting that controversial vote, City Council leaders have <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/city-hall/2026/09/15/parking-meters-deal-stonepeak-partners-chicago-city-council-brandon-johnson-pat-dowell" >brokered a compromise</a> to try to level the playing field for Chicago taxpayers. What changes did they make? Why is the parking meters deal so controversial? Here's what you need to know: </p><h3>What was so bad about the 2008 parking meters deal?</h3><h3></h3><p>In 2008, then-Mayor Richard M. Daley leased the city’s 36,000 parking meters for 75 years to a private investment consortium for $1.15 billion. He used those proceeds to avoid raising property taxes at a time when city employee pension funds were sinking deeper in the hole. </p><p>The lopsided deal sold off an asset that was generating revenue for the city. Motorists paid the price with steep rate hikes. The Chicago Parking Meters LLC consortium formed by Morgan Stanley, Allianz and Sovereign Wealth recouped their initial $1.15 billion investment by 2019 — roughly 11 years into the 75-year lease.</p><p>Steep rate increases built into the deal would have been bad enough. Rates downtown, for example, rose from $3 an hour in 2008 to $6.50 an hour in 2013. But broken and frozen pay-and-display boxes, along with overstuffed and improperly calibrated meters that overcharged motorists, made it even worse.</p><p>Some motorists were so incensed they vandalized meters and boycotted metered parking, leading to a dramatic drop in on-street parking.</p><p>The deal also required the city to compensate Chicago Parking Meters LLC for every parking space taken out of service, either for a special event or construction project. That part of the deal alone has tied the city’s hands and cost Chicago taxpayers tens of millions of dollars.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-890000" name="image-890000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/d9f8b2a/2147483647/strip/true/crop/2000x1122+0+137/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fd2%2F5d%2Ff1b58a944391b54ba7af8cb56a4a%2Fbig-box-ordinance.JPG 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/423a454/2147483647/strip/true/crop/2000x1122+0+137/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fd2%2F5d%2Ff1b58a944391b54ba7af8cb56a4a%2Fbig-box-ordinance.JPG 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/27d126e/2147483647/strip/true/crop/2000x1122+0+137/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fd2%2F5d%2Ff1b58a944391b54ba7af8cb56a4a%2Fbig-box-ordinance.JPG" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="Richard M. Daley at City Hall" srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/27d126e/2147483647/strip/true/crop/2000x1122+0+137/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fd2%2F5d%2Ff1b58a944391b54ba7af8cb56a4a%2Fbig-box-ordinance.JPG 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/2425424/2147483647/strip/true/crop/2000x1122+0+137/resize/980x550!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fd2%2F5d%2Ff1b58a944391b54ba7af8cb56a4a%2Fbig-box-ordinance.JPG 2x" width="490" height="275" data-src="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/27d126e/2147483647/strip/true/crop/2000x1122+0+137/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fd2%2F5d%2Ff1b58a944391b54ba7af8cb56a4a%2Fbig-box-ordinance.JPG" data-lazy-load="true" src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" > </picture> <div class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Then-Mayor Richard M. Daley, shown at a City Council meeting in 2006.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>M. Spencer Green/Associated Press </p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p> Daley muscled the deal through the City Council with only five dissenting votes and little debate. But he was forced to acknowledge City Hall botched the transition to private control, and that the turnover should have taken place over a three-to-six month period instead of all at once.</p><p></p><p>No issue in recent memory — not even the Hired Truck and city hiring scandals or <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/politics/2026/09/11/mayor-daley-meigs-field-closure-terrorism-no-fly-zones-northerly-island" >Daley’s notorious midnight destruction of Meigs Field</a> — has resonated more with voters than the parking meter deal.</p><p></p><p></p><p></p><h3>What must the Chicago City Council decide now?</h3><p>After making a killing, private investors from as far away as Abu Dhabi wanted out and invited bids for Chicago's parking meters.</p><p>Without consulting the Council, Mayor Brandon Johnson submitted a $3.2 billion bid that turned out to be hundreds of millions of dollars higher than the competition.</p><p>But the mayor ultimately abandoned the offer after determining the risk of undoing the parking meter deal was not worth the reward, either financially or politically.</p><p>It would have required the city to pledge to siphon other major sources of revenue the city depends on “if parking habits shifted, alternative modes of transportation become more common” or if parking and commuting habits changed.</p><p>That’s a distinct possibility amid a fast-changing landscape for parking demand that includes everything from self-driving vehicles and robot delivery to congestion fees that discourage people from driving downtown.</p><p>After the city dropped out, New York investment firm Stonepeak Partners emerged as the winner with a $2.53 billion bid, pending City Council approval by a revised, Sept. 30 deadline.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" class="Figure-credit"><p>Pat Nabong/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>With no direction from the mayor, Finance Chair Pat Dowell (3rd) said she and other other veteran alderpersons “took the bull by the horns and did the work” to try and, as she put it, “make lemonade out of lemons.” They negotiated an agreement that calls for the city to receive a $75 million transfer fee at closing and 5% of net income going forward — or $376.2 million over the course of the agreement.</p><p>It also would reduce costly compensation the city is required to pay for every space taken out of service.</p><p>Stonepeak has also agreed to sell Omni Air International, an airline that has provided long-haul deportation flights for the Department of Homeland Security during President Donald Trump’s deportation campaign. And it has agreed to explore creating entire non-metered city blocks as “potential electric vehicle charging stations with charging revenues shared with the city.”</p><p></p><p>The $75 million up-front payment and offer of future profit-sharing may not be enough to garner the 26 votes needed for passage.</p><p>With aldermanic elections less than five months away, some alderpersons may want to push the envelope to see if they get some kind of a break for motorists.</p><p>“City Council members who we’ve been in contact with are still talking. They might be looking at certain points saying, `Hey maybe can we sweeten here, sweeten there?’“ senior mayoral adviser <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/city-hall/2026/09/17/chicago-parking-meter-compromise-stonepeak-partners-city-council-mayoral-adviser-jason-lee" >Jason Lee told the Sun-Times. </a>“But in general, the idea that, if you’re going to approve that … you’re going to get concessions that are better for the taxpayers — obviously that is something that we believe is the right direction.”</p><p></p><p></p><h3>What happens if the Council does not approve the compromise deal?</h3><p>The risk to Chicago taxpayers is great. It could cost the city millions.</p><p>The Morgan Stanley-led investment group could first ask an independent arbitrator to order the City Council to approve the sale or pay an exorbitant penalty, then file a lawsuit.</p><p>Former U.S. Attorney Dan Webb, who represents the investment group, wrote a letter to the mayor in June warning the city could face “financial catastrophe” if the sale to Stonepeak Partners is rejected.</p><p>“If the city breaches” the 75-year lease “with the result that the sale to Stonepeak collapses, that will destroy value measures in the billions of dollars for which the city will be held legally responsible,” Webb wrote in the letter.</p><h3>Is that an idle threat? </h3><h3></h3><p>No, it isn’t. Last year, Chicago taxpayers were forced to spend $15.5 million to compensate the investment team that leased the meters, thanks to a risky pandemic-era scheme authorized by former Mayor Lori Lightfoot. As bitter a pill as that was for Chicagoans who despise the deal, it could have been a whole lot worse. The investment group started out by seeking $322 million from the city. An arbitrator recommended $120.7 million. The fact that the Johnson administration managed to persuade Chicago Parking Meters LLC to accept $15.5 million — just 12.8 % of the original demand — was a victory, even though it didn’t seem like it.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-140000" name="image-140000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/7c37352/2147483647/strip/true/crop/8192x4598+0+433/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F78%2F55%2Fa2194e5a4e739bbcba8393c31a97%2Fmayorannounces-260914-004.JPG 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/376249e/2147483647/strip/true/crop/8192x4598+0+433/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F78%2F55%2Fa2194e5a4e739bbcba8393c31a97%2Fmayorannounces-260914-004.JPG 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/d96647f/2147483647/strip/true/crop/8192x4598+0+433/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F78%2F55%2Fa2194e5a4e739bbcba8393c31a97%2Fmayorannounces-260914-004.JPG" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="Mayor Brandon Johnson announces his bid for re-election Sunday at DuSable Black History Museum Sunday. After abandoning the city’s bid, Johnson washed his hands of the matter and threw the political hot potato in the City Council’s lap. He gave the Council no direction, possibly concerned there could be political blowback — no matter which way the Council votes.</p><p></p><p></p><p></p><p></p>

entries.title: Man charged after June Kenwood shooting that seriously injured a 15-year-old boy
entries.summary: <p>A 48-year-old Chicago man has been charged with attempted murder after shooting at three people, including a 15-year-old boy who was seriously wounded in June in the Kenwood neighborhood. </p><p>Shauntay Sardin, 48, was charged with three counts of attempted murder because there were two additional victims who were not shot, and aggravated battery, police said.</p><p>On June 20 in the 700 block of East 47th Street, Sardin allegedly opened fire at three people, including a 15-year-old boy who was shot and seriously injured, police said. </p><p>Sardin, of the 1900 block of East 72nd Place in South Shore and who was arrested Monday in the 5100 block of South Indiana Avenue, was due for a detention hearing Tuesday at the Leighton Criminal Courthouse <br><b> </b></p>

target="_blank" >Despite data center hate, local government agency sees dollar signs</a></h3><p></p><h5>Reporting by <a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-ydjridll-l-i/" target="_blank" >Brett Chase</a></h5><p><b>Highly hated</b>: Polls show data centers are widely hated. But the government body that oversees Cook County’s sewer system and manages stormwater sees data centers for artificial intelligence as an opportunity to pad its almost $2 billion, largely taxpayer-funded, annual budget.</p><p><b>Data center drive</b>: The Metropolitan Water Reclamation District of Greater Chicago, the owner of the Deep Tunnel flood-control system, stands to bring in millions of dollars in potential new revenue if it can sell treated sewer water to data centers and other industrial companies. Data centers — being built at a rapid pace to support artificial intelligence — present a timely opportunity.</p><p><b>Zooming in</b>: Americans are skeptical about AI's benefits and are feeling a growing — largely bipartisan — dislike of data centers in particular. Almost 60% of people surveyed said they were concerned about the impact on water supply, while an even greater number voiced alarm about the effect on electricity prices, according to a recent University of Chicago poll.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-ydjridll-l-d/" target="_blank" ><b>READ MORE</b></a></p><hr><p></p><h4>GRAVE INJUSTICE ✶</h4><div class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-ydjridll-l-tu/" target="_blank" >Erica Thompson</a></h5><p>If you name any gospel music star of the mid-20th century, Gregory Donald Gay probably has a story about them. As the younger brother of the Gay Sisters gospel trio, he had a front-row seat for the action during gospel's golden age.</p><p>Now, he is sharing his tales in a recently released book, "Can I Get a Witness! Faith, Family and Chicago Gospel Music" (The University of Chicago Press). The text was co-written with Steven B. Dolins, the 69-year-old founder and president of The Sirens Records music label in Highland Park.</p><p>Gay's late siblings — Evelyn, Geraldine and Mildred — performed, recorded or rubbed elbows with Clara Ward, Mahalia Jackson, Sam Cooke, the Staple Singers, James Cleveland, Sister Rosetta Tharpe, Dizzy Gillespie and Sonny Rollins.</p><p>They released music on the legendary Savoy, Decca and Chess labels, toured the country and helped bring gospel to a televised audience. Their 1951 hit record, "God Will Take Care of You," was later covered by Aretha Franklin.</p><p>But their accomplishments have been overlooked, and their records are difficult to find beyond streaming sites or YouTube.</p><p>Gay said his late sisters would have been forgotten without Dolins.</p><p>"I’m grateful for him opening up a window and letting the general public look in," Gay said.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-ydjridll-l-il/" target="_blank" ><b>READ MORE</b></a></p><hr><p></p><h4>YOUR DAILY QUESTION ☕️</h4><p><b>What's your favorite part about fall in Chicago? Tell us why.</b></p><p><a class="Link" href="mailto:newsletters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" ><i>Reply to this question via email</i></a><i> (please include your first and last name). We may run your answer in a future newsletter or story.</i></p><p>On Monday, we asked you: <a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-ydjridll-l-iy/" target="_blank" >What was the last truly no-phones performance you attended</a></p><p>Here’s some of what you said, edited for length and clarity.</p><p>"Chris Rock several times." — <i>Pat Friedlander</i></p><p>"Jill Scott, Aug. 2026. They put phones in a locked bag that you could hold onto." — <i>Tim Thomas</i></p><p>"Jack White in 2022 at UIC. Slowed down things getting in and out, but in general no phones once you were in was good. I could see it being problematic, though. If my parents needed to reach us about a babysitting issue, there would have been no good way to do it." — <i>Arcadia Kust McCauley</i></p><p>"The Paper Machete variety show held at Green Mill every Saturday afternoon is a 'no video, no photo' event. It is refreshing to watch the show without the distraction of a phone held up and blocking the view. The crowd is 'in the moment,' as it should be." — <i>Jimmy Pobol</i></p><p>"Friday night at the Vic - Gary Clark Jr. The Yonder pouches were in use. It was fine. I miss not being able to take video of the show though." — <i>Chris Perez</i></p><p>"Well, <a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-ydjridll-l-ij/" target="_blank" >Phoebe Bridgers</a>. But before that, it was probably farm aid in the late 1990s. It was wonderful and a good learning experience of better communication for my daughter and her friends. It was a joy to watch her express real emotions and soak in the live music she loves so much." — <i>Hope Zawaski</i></p><hr><p>Thanks for reading the Sun-Times Morning Edition!<br>Got a story you think we missed? <a class="Link" href="mailto:newsletters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" >Email us here.</a></p><hr><p><b>Written and curated by</b>: Matt Moore<br><b>Editor</b>: Michael Lansu</p>

entries.title: Is it OK for adults to wear pajamas in public?
entries.summary: <p>Lately I've been walking down the street in my pajamas.</p><p>Not regularly. A couple of times.</p><p>OK, four. Maybe five.</p><p>Which might be a cause for concern, right? Older guy, strolling the neighborhood in his pj's. One immediately thinks of Vincent Gigante, the Genovese crime family boss who wandered Greenwich Village for 30 years in a robe, pajamas and slippers. Pretending to be crazy, trying to build an insanity defense and keep himself out of jail.</p><p>Not the best company to be in (plus it didn't work; he died in prison).</p><p>So what's my excuse?</p><p>Well, I have a few — not excuses — but reasons.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-500000" name="module-500000"></a> <div class="RichTextSidebarModule-title">Opinion bug</div> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h2>Opinion</h2></div> </div><p>First Kitty, our elderly dog. She's 16, or 112 in human years. Without going into detail, her habits are changing. While she used to be a regular 7 a.m., 5 p.m. and 9 p.m. kind of gal, now she might feel the urge at 1:30 a.m., or 3 a.m., or 5 a.m. or, one recent night, 1:30 <i>and </i>3 <i>and</i> 5 a.m.</p><p>Let's put it this way — right now my wife is in Washington, D.C., enjoying grandchildren No. 1 and No. 3, while I'm here, tending to a dog. Because we just couldn't hand the dog to a neighbor with a wave and a breezy — "Oh, by the way, you might need to walk her every two hours, bye!" — as we waltz out the door.</p><p>Second, let me tell you something about Center Avenue. It isn't like strolling Michigan Avenue in your jammies, though I imagine that happens. Not many people at noon. At 5 a.m. it's pretty much me. So far, this fashion leap is only taken at night.</p><p>Third, the shoulder surgery, while healing nicely, two months on, still makes slipping off a pajama top, half asleep, a fraught endeavor, particularly if the room is dark and your dog is emitting an urgent "Let's go NOW!" whine.</p><p>Once, I didn't even bother with shoes. I don't think I've ever walked down my block barefoot before. First time for everything. Nobody cared, including me. The glory of age. Heretofore really important stuff? Not so bleepin' important anymore. </p><p>Fourth, in my defense, they're good pj's — J. Crew. Quality stuff. Not raggedy. One reason the pajamas are in such good shape is because I own many pairs. I like various shades and swoop in on sales. I went on the J. Crew site to see what's new, pajama-wise, and noticed this description: "Your go-to pant for hanging out, walking the dog or watching the game." </p><p>See? I'm backed up by catalog copy, the definition of middle-class respectability. Because really, when was the last time a catalog suggested doing something wrong? "You'll silently slide down boutique aisles, shoplifting, in these natural suede Roland loafers by Rockport ..."</p><p>Trendsetters add support. Neil Pasricha,wildly popular author of best-sellers like "The Happiness Equation," "You Are Awesome" and "Our Book of Awesome," and similar quality fare, has a blog "1,000 Awesome Things" including, "<a class="Link" href="https://1000awesomethings.com/2011/02/17/306-wearing-pajamas-outside-of-the-house/" target="_blank" >#306 Wearing pajamas outside of the house” </a>which states, "wearing pajamas outside of the house is such a great move. It’s like you’re finally admitting to yourself that being comfy is worth it."</p><p>He lists situations where the practice is especially awesome, including:</p><p>"3. Walking the dog. Whether it’s the midnight stroll in the dead of winter or the early morning walk before the sun comes up, it’s always a classy move to roam the hood in pajamas, a tattered robe, and maybe some furry pink earmuffs."</p><p>The furry pink earmuffs make me wonder if he's being 100% sincere. But given that No. 154 is "Reading an actual newspaper," I'm willing to give Pasricha the benefit of the doubt, even though he thinks he's describing an arcane practice from a "long, long time ago," as if he were talking about churning butter. He redeems himself with the sentiment: "maybe you connected with the columnists. You learned from them, were challenged by them, and read everything they wrote."</p><p>See? You're doing something right now that others can only pine for.</p><p>Delving into fashion journalism, it seems pajamas are best worn in public by children up late or freshmen up early.</p><p>Older men, well, not so much We don't look as good in pajamas. Or rather, if we wear them, we are expected to be shuffling along a ward somewhere. Maybe the problem is wearing anything else. I need to buy a fez, upgrade my brand of pajama — something silky and stylish — and claim it's some kind of cultural statement. Who would dare question my preferred method of life? Of course, to do that, they'd first have to notice or care, and the only person who does either is in D.C. all week.</p>

entries.title: Después del Operativo Midway Blitz, algunos prometen permanecer en La Villita, otros temen no poder
entries.summary: <p>La Villita afrontaba presiones de desplazamiento y gentrificación mucho antes del Operativo Midway Blitz, donde en 2024 casi la mitad de los inquilinos destinaban más del 30% de sus ingresos en la vivienda. La proximidad del vecindario al centro y la rápida gentrificación de Pilsen —los límites aproximados de Pilsen también alimentaron la preocupación de que el desarrollo pueda expulsar a residentes y negocios de toda la vida.</p><p>La pandemia de COVID-19 provocó otro periodo de desestabilización, obligando a cerrar a algunos negocios y dejando a otros en apuros.</p><p>Luego vino la campaña masiva de deportaciones del presidente Donald Trump.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-4b0000" name="module-4b0000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>La Voz Chicago WhatsApp</h3>Encuentra más noticias en nuestro canal de WhatsApp. <a class="Link" href="https://www.whatsapp.com/channel/0029Vb0XT1XCHDylm3rCs40P" target="_blank" ><b>Síguenos.</b></a></div> </div><p>Durante el punto álgido del Operativo Midway Blitz, agentes federales de inmigración detuvieron a 3,841 personas, según datos federales analizados por el Chicago Sun-Times y WBEZ.</p><p>La Villita se convirtió en uno de los blancos más visibles. Agentes federales hicieron detenciones en el vecindario en el primer día completo de Midway Blitz y regresaron repetidamente en los meses siguientes.</p><p>El 22 y 23 de octubre y de nuevo el 8 de noviembre, grandes grupos de agentes federales descendieron sobre La Villita, realizando arrestos y confrontando residentes y manifestantes. La <a class="Link" href="https://ilac.illinois.gov/content/dam/soi/en/web/ilac/documents/final-report/inv-briefs/IAC-Little-Village-Investigation-Brief-r.pdf" target="_blank" >Comisión de Responsabilidad de Illinois</a> más tarde señaló esos tres días para una investigación de lo que describió como una “ocupación” del vecindario.</p><p>Los efectos fueron más allá de los arrestos. El miedo a los agentes de inmigración mantuvo a la gente en casa. Tiendas y restaurantes se vaciaron, golpeando los corredores comerciales de La Villita. Un <a class="Link" href="https://greatcities.uic.edu/news-stories/hunkering-down-the-hidden-economic-cost-of-federal-immigration-enforcement-in-cook-county-il/" target="_blank" >análisis de la University of Illinois Chicago</a> publicado este mes estimó que el aumento de la aplicación de la ley de inmigración iniciado en enero de 2025 resultó en $1,260 millones en pérdida de actividad al por menor y de restaurantes en el Condado de Cook durante el año siguiente. Los investigadores dijeron que los residentes de vecindarios con un gran número de personas “nacidas en Latinoamérica” asistieron menos a tiendas y restaurantes fuera de sus comunidades, una caída que se prolongó casi un año.</p><p>La aplicación de la ley migratoria es ahora más silenciosa y menos visible, pero la administración de Trump continúa arrestando a cientos de personas cada mes.</p><p>En La Villita, muchos siguen quedándose en casa, y algunos dueños de negocios están gastando ahorros acumulados por generaciones para mantenerse abiertos. Algunos se preguntan si podrán permitirse quedarse.</p><p>El Sun-Times habló con residentes, dueños de negocios y una agente inmobiliaria del vecindario sobre cómo la aplicación de la ley de inmigración está impactando a La Villita: afectando negocios, atrayendo ofertas por propiedades y llevando a algunos residentes a invertir en regresar a México y reevaluar su futuro en Chicago.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-8619c2" name="image-8619c2"></a> <picture class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Anthony Vazquez/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p></p><h3>Luchó contra el desplazamiento. Ahora se pregunta si puede quedarse</h3><p>María de la Luz Rodríguez, de 61 años de edad, quien vive en La Villita desde hace 19 años, empezó a trabajar con la cooperativa de vivienda <a class="Link" href="https://www.lavillitahousingcoop.com/" target="_blank" >Cooperativa La Villita</a> tras ver edificios de departamentos cambiar de dueño y a inquilinos ser desplazados. Originaria de Veracruz, México, Rodríguez ayudó a elaborar y redactar los estatutos de la cooperativa en español e inglés, repartió folletos y habló en reuniones comunitarias.</p><p>Finalmente, la cooperativa compró su primer edificio, una propiedad de seis unidades en Whipple Street. Según su sitio web, los cargos mensuales estimados por vivienda oscilan entre $950 y $1,150. Para este verano, dice Rodríguez, todos sus apartamentos estaban ocupados y el grupo trabajaba para comprar otro.</p><p>“La cooperativa es un grupo de gente que realmente ama La Villita”, dice Rodríguez en español.</p><p>Pero Rodríguez, que no tiene estatus legal, afirma que su propia posibilidad de permanecer en La Villita se ha vuelto incierta. Perdió su empleo en el comercio al por menor después de que su empleador comenzara a usar el sistema federal E-Verify para verificar si el personal estaba autorizado para trabajar en Estados Unidos.</p><p>Planeaba comprar una membresía de la cooperativa pero no pudo hacerlo tras quedarse desempleada. Sigue siendo voluntaria como miembro de la junta directiva.</p><p>También perdió trabajo como promotora de salud comunitaria cuando se agotaron los fondos. Ahora lucha por pagar su renta.</p><p>La venta ambulante se ha convertido en una forma de salir adelante. La Asociación de Vendedores Ambulantes de Chicago le dio $500 de ayuda. Carga buñuelos y cacahuates estilo Veracruz en una maleta y lleva su mercancía a ferias comunitarias y de salud porque hay más gente que en el corredor comercial de La Villita.</p><p>“La Villita está muerta”, dice.</p><p>Rodríguez afirma que la gente de La Villita no quiere irse. Los vecinos se cuidan unos a otros.</p><p>No obstante, ella misma está considerando marcharse.</p><p>Rodríguez tiene familia en México y está pensando en regresar a Veracruz. “Puede que no haya mucho propietarios en La Villita durante años. La agente de RE/MAX dice que las familias suelen mantener sus propiedades por décadas, lo que resulta en poca rotación.</p><p>Pero Villegas está viendo a algunas familias inmigrantes considerar un futuro distinto.</p><p>Villegas dice que ha trabajado con varios clientes de La Villita que han invertido en inmuebles en México, incluidas familias que buscan un posible lugar para vivir en el futuro. Los promotores inmobiliarios con los que trabaja están principalmente en ciudades mexicanas más grandes, pero cree que las familias de La Villita que realmente regresen a México podrían volver a sus lugares de origen.</p><p>Hay otras señales de que más familias del área de Chicago tienen a México en mente. Las solicitudes en el Consulado de México en Chicago para registrar a personas nacidas en Estados Unidos como mexicanas más que se duplicaron, de 3,800 en 2024 a 9,646 en 2025, según el consulado.</p><p>A través de la red de Villegas, terrenos pueden empezar en unos $35,000, condominios en $100,000 y casas en $135,000.</p><p>“No sabes cómo va a ser el futuro por la política actual, y lo que seguirá haciendo a las familias a largo plazo”, dice.</p><p>Villegas ha construido una red de contactos en México que puede ayudar a los clientes a encontrar vivienda, iniciar negocios y ganarse la vida. Para las familias que consideran irse de Estados Unidos, dice, su trabajo no es simplemente vender su casa sino ayudarlas a planear lo que viene después.</p><p>“¿Cuál es el plan?”, dice, “y ¿cómo podemos llevarlos a ese plan?”.</p><p>Villegas afirma que alguien que ha pagado una casa durante décadas podría comprar una casa por mucho menos en partes de México y vivir con lo que quede.</p><p>Pero se ha encontrado con propietarios dispuestos a aceptar ofertas no solicitadas antes de darse cuenta de que podrían estar perdiendo $50,000, $60,000 o $70,000 de plusvalía.</p><p>La decisión de comprar en México rara vez se debe a una sola razón, dice. Un propietario puede lidiar con problemas con inquilinos, costos de reparación de edificios o un negocio que está navegando. El estatus migratorio puede hacer más difícil resolver esos problemas.</p><p>Eventualmente, dice Villegas, las presiones pueden acumularse.</p><p>“A veces la gente simplemente también está cansada”, afirma. “A veces la gente ya no tiene la voluntad de luchar”.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" clientes</h3><p>Alrededor de la 1 p.m. del 13 de agosto, el Restaurante Los Candiles, en 2624 S. Central Ave., estaba casi vacío.</p><p>José Luis (Louie) López estaba allí con un trabajador de cocina y su esposa, Clarita López, de 40 años, quien atiende mesas. Había muchas mesas pero pocos clientes.</p><p>López, de 44 años, sacó los calendarios de papel que guarda para anotar el número de pedidos de cocina que el restaurante atiende cada día. Antes de la pandemia, el restaurante registraba típicamente entre 40 y 50 pedidos de cocina entre semana. Los sábados podían llegar a 90. Los domingos, ayudados por el flujo de feligreses, podían alcanzar los 110.</p><p>Señaló el calendario de este año. Un martes tuvo 12 pedidos. Otro día 14. Los sábados que antes llegaban a 90 ahora están en los 30.</p><p>“Todo está a la mitad”, dice López.</p><p>Sus padres abrieron Los Candiles en 1995. La familia es dueña del edificio y terminó de pagarlo hace aproximadamente una década. Eso le ha ahorrado a López un pago de renta o hipoteca mientras el negocio cae.</p><p>Pero ser dueño del edificio no ha traído clientes a la puerta.</p><p>López dice que la aplicación de la ley migratoria es solo una parte de lo que ha perjudicado al restaurante. Los costos de los alimentos han subido y los clientes tienen menos dinero para gastar. Cuando corren rumores de que los agentes de inmigración han regresado, dice, la gente vuelve a asustarse.</p><p>Para sobrellevarlo, cada vez más ha sacado a Los Candiles fuera de La Villita.</p><p>López empezó a ofrecer taquizas en 2017. Lleva una plancha, arroz y frijoles, tortillas y charolas de guarniciones y cocina para los clientes en el lugar.</p><p>“Eso es lo que nos mantiene a flote”, dice López.</p><p>Se acercó a Cody’s Public House, un bar en Lakeview, con la idea de vender tacos allí los jueves. La relación eventualmente se convirtió en un trabajo semanal.</p><p>López dice que Los Candiles puede vender más tacos en cuatro horas en Cody’s que en siete horas en el restaurante de La para de moverse. El presidente del Little Village Community Council va de una conversación a otra con la gente que busca consejo y ayuda en su oficina. Hay útiles escolares y pañales para quienes lo necesitan. Cuando los agentes de inmigración comenzaron a operar intensamente en La Villita el otoño pasado, se convirtió en uno de los organizadores más visibles del vecindario, advirtiendo a residentes sobre avistamientos reportados de ICE y ayudando a coordinar la respuesta comunitaria.</p><p>También es dueño de un edificio de cinco unidades en la cuadra 2300 al sur de Trumbull Ave.</p><p>Las consultas inmobiliarias no solicitadas sobre su propiedad no son nuevas. Enriquez dice que comenzaron a aumentar durante la pandemia de COVID-19. Pero desde el pasado otoño tras el Operativo Midway Blitz se han vuelto mucho más frecuentes.</p><p>“Recibo correo, llamadas telefónicas, correos electrónicos”, dice Enriquez. Algunos días, Enriquez estima que recibe hasta 30 solicitudes. Algunos preguntan si quiero vender. Otros ofrecen financiamiento. Ha guardado capturas de pantalla de mensajes de texto de personas preguntando por su propiedad, así como un envío por correo de finales de agosto de Sherman Property, un negocio comprador de casas en efectivo, diseñado para parecer un cheque a su nombre por $316,222.</p><p>Dice que compradores potenciales le han ofrecido hasta $1 millón por su edificio. Ha rechazado las ofertas.</p><p>Uno de sus inquilinos, un adulto mayor que vive en el edificio desde hace 15 años, aún paga $800 al mes por un apartamento de tres habitaciones. Enriquez dice que el hombre le ha dicho que si la renta subiera tendría que irse y empezar de nuevo en otro lugar, lejos de los doctores y del vecindario que conoce. Dice que un nuevo propietario podría cobrar $1,300 o $1,500 por la misma unidad.</p><p>Los negocios de La Villita todavía se están recuperando de meses en que los clientes se quedaron en casa en medio de los controles migratorios. Los propietarios enfrentan impuestos más altos y los costos de mantener edificios envejecidos. Los operativos de ICE, cree, empeoraron la situación.</p><p>“Le echaron más gasolina”, afirma.</p><p>Enriquez ha pasado años tratando de construir una vida, inversiones y un futuro en La Villita. class="Figure-credit"><p>Anthony Vazquez/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p></p><h3>El costo de quedarse</h3><p>Alrededor de las 4 p.m. del 13 de agosto, Osito’s Tap estaba tranquilo y con poca luz. Alguien arreglaba botellas de licor mientras Mike Moreno Jr., 35 años, se sentaba en una mesa cercana. Los primeros clientes aún no habían llegado.</p><p>La familia Moreno ha hecho negocios en La Villita por más de medio siglo. Su abuelo operaba tiendas de abarrotes en el vecindario y su padre abrió Moreno’s Liquors en la calle 26 en 1977. Moreno más tarde abrió Osito’s Tap cerca de la intersección de la calle 26 y Ridgeway.</p><p>La familia ha sobrevivido tiempos difíciles antes, incluida la pandemia de COVID-19. Pero Moreno dice que los operativos de control migratorio trajeron otro tipo de tensión.</p><p>De agosto a noviembre del año pasado, el negocio en Osito’s y Moreno’s Liquors cayó a la mitad durante dos meses y al menos un 25% durante los otros dos, dice Moreno. La familia recortó gastos y amplió la entrega a domicilio. Evitaron despidos.</p><p>También empezaron a gastar sus ahorros.</p><p>“Literalmente los estamos tomando de generaciones y generaciones, años y años de ahorros que construimos, y simplemente reinvirtiéndolos y volviéndolos a poner en nuestros propios negocios”, dice Moreno.</p><p>La familia de Moreno tiene propiedades en La Villita y no tiene la intención de vender. Pero dice que las indagaciones de especuladores se han vuelto cada vez más difíciles de ignorar.</p><p>Antes de los arrestos de ICE, dice Moreno, podía recibir cuatro o cinco llamadas a la semana de personas interesadas en comprar su propiedad u ofrecer financiamiento. Ahora, a veces recibe cuatro o cinco en un día.</p><p>Moreno cuenta que alguien le dijo que había visto informes mediáticos sobre las redadas y su impacto económico en los negocios de La Villita antes de preguntar por su propiedad.</p><p>Usualmente bloquea los números.</p><p>“No vamos a vender”, dice Moreno. “Hemos estado aquí casi 50 años, y estaremos aquí otros 50”.</p><p>“Mientras trabajemos muy duro”, dice Moreno, “podremos mantener lo nuestro”.</p><p><i>Traducido con una herramienta de inteligencia artificial (IA) y editado por los seres humanos de</i> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/la-voz" target="_blank" ><i>La Voz Chicago</i></a><br></p>

entries.title: Batavia and Geneva match up for the 108th time; Simeon-Morgan Park showdown set for the West Side
entries.summary: <p>Geneva vs. Batavia will always be one of the state’s special rivalries. On Sunday, Batavia sent out a 45-page PDF documenting the rivalry's history, which began in 1913.</p><p>The schools have not played every year since then, but both have a long, interesting football history. Records show a game between Geneva and a combined team from West Batavia and East Batavia in 1896.</p><p>Geneva holds a slight edge overall, winning 52 of the rivalry games and losing 50. There have been five ties.</p><p>In all those years, there are likely few times when both teams have been so highly regarded around the state and so likely to put up a massive point total.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/super-25-football-rankings/2026/09/20/high-school-football-rankings-chicago-illinois-sun-times-michael-obrien" >No. 6 Batavia</a> (4-1) is averaging 45 points and No. 16 Geneva (4-1) is posting 38 points per game. And neither team has a lockdown defense, so expect a lot of points on the scoreboard Friday night in Batavia.</p><p>The Bulldogs gained 536 yards against St. Charles North in Week 5. Quarterback Michael Vander Luitgaren, a Wyoming recruit, has completed 77% of his passes this season and thrown for 1,509 yards with 19 touchdowns and four interceptions. Darin Ashiru, a Western Michigan recruit, is averaging 119 receiving yards per game.</p><p>Geneva’s Ben Peterson and Bennett Konkey may be the top quarterback-wide receiver duo in the area, a massive statement given the receiver talent at Mount Carmel.</p><p>Peterson is 87-for-124, throwing for 1,607 yards and 19 touchdowns with just one interception. The 6-5 senior is heading to Eastern Michigan. Konkey, an Illinois recruit, has 40 catches for 886 yards and 12 TDs. The track star is one of the area’s most exciting players.</p><p>At some point, one of the defenses will have to step up with a stop or a turnover, and that will likely be the game's key play.</p><h3>South Side showdown on the West Side</h3><p>Saturday’s big rivalry game is Morgan Park vs. Simeon … at Rockne Stadium on the West Side. Hopefully the odd location doesn’t keep fans away.</p><p>With Gately Stadium still being redone, Rockne’s size and parking probably make it the most sensible location. It is large enough to hold a good crowd, and the parking situation has improved since the stadium was refurbished a few years ago.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/high-school-football/2026/09/19/king-football-simeon-chicago" >King’s upset of Simeon</a> took some of the luster off this game, but also adds to the Wolverines’ desperation for a victory. Simeon (1-4) has shown flashes of real potential but has yet to put together a complete game against a quality team.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" The Mustangs gave undefeated No. 10 Dowers Grove North its toughest test of the season, losing 17-12 in the suburbs.</p><p>“Overall, I would argue this might be the best group we have had as far as all the different factors: talent, togetherness, understanding,” Morgan Park coach Chris James said. “And we are a lot better as coaches.”</p><h3>TikTok Talk</h3><p>Social media has been around for a while, but something about TikTok has led to an explosion of high school football trash talk. Throughout the city and suburbs, players are mentioning after games how much back-and-forth there is between the teams during the week on the social media app.</p><p>One Simeon player returned to the sideline last weekend in the game against King and tried to rally his teammates by yelling “this isn’t Tik Tok anymore, we are here now.”</p>
