entries.title: More Bears QB woes as Tyson Bagent placed in concussion protocol
entries.summary: <p>The only healthy quarterback on the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Bears</a>' active roster is 38 and hasn't thrown a regular-season pass since 2023.</p><p>The <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/09/22/caleb-williams-injury-bears-eagles-mnf-chicago-philadelphia-vikings-soldier-field-nfl" target="_blank" >Bears</a>' complicated quarterback situation grew even more so Tuesday afternoon, when a source confirmed that backup quarterback Tyson Bagent had been placed in the NFL's concussion protocol. That lines up veteran Case Keenum to start Monday night against the Eagles in the event Bagent can't clear the protocol in time.</p><p>Caleb Williams pulled his right hamstring Sunday against the Vikings. He won’t practice this week. While coach Ben Johnson wouldn’t rule him out for the Eagles game, his participation seems unlikely. </p><p>Bagent was likely to make his first start since his rookie year in replacing Williams. That was thrown into question Tuesday, however, when word spread about his place in the protocol. He'll have one extra day to get ready, though, as the Bears don't play until Sept. 28. </p><p>Bagent was hit with force twice after taking over for Williams midway through the fourth quarter. He was struck in the head by outside linebacker Andrew Van Ginkel after throwing incomplete when he rolled left on third-and-goal from the Vikings’ 5. The Vikings blocked a field goal on the next play. Bagent was also thrown to the ground by outside linebacker Dallas Turner on the game-ending sack, but appeared to land on his left shoulder. </p><p>Keenum has started four games this decade — two for the Texans in 2023 and two for the Browns in 2021. He's been the third-stringer during Ben Johnson's two years with the Bears. General manager Ryan Poles regretted not having a veteran presence for Williams when he was a rookie and considered Keenum a perfect choice. Williams, who considers Keenum to have the smartest football mind among Bears players, lives in the same neighborhood as the veteran.</p><p>Keenum has started 66 NFL games in a career that started in 2013. The odds of him starting another one, though, were slim until this week.</p><p>The Bears think of Bagent as one of the best 32 quarterbacks in the NFL, though. Poles and Bears coach Ben Johnson gave him a two-year, $10 million contract extension a year ago that keeps him with the Bears through next season. They rebuffed trade offers for Bagent this spring.</p><p>Bagent could still practice this week. The Vikings’ Kyler Murray was limited in practices all last week despite being in the concussion protocol. He didn't play against the Bears but was announced as this week's starter.</p><p>It will be instructive to see whether the Bears add another quarterback to their roster this week. They have Miller Moss, who spent all training camp as the fourth-stringer, on their practice squad. If Williams and Bagent sit out, Moss would serve as the second-stringer. The team would still likely need an emergency quarterback who wouldn't count against their game-day roster total but could enter the game if two quarterbacks were hurt against the Eagles.</p><p>It's unclear when Bagent reported the concussion. Johnson treated Bagent as the Bears' next option Monday, saying he felt "strongly about what [Bagent] is capable of — and our team does, too." He then weaved in Keenum's name, too. </p><p>"Him and Case both have won games in this league," Johnson said. "There's a lot of confidence that both of those guys can get the job done if it comes to it.”</p><p>The NFL’s return-to-participation protocol features five steps. There's no set timeline required for any one step.</p><p>The player is initially prescribed rest and told to avoid physical and mental activities that aggravate the concussion. They can still stretch and do balance training.<br>In Phase 2, they can ramp up exercise and stretching. Phases 3 and 4 allow the player do exercises in practice and participate in non-contact drills, respectively. Once the team clears the player for full contact, the player must be cleared by an independent neurological consultant in order to play in a game.</p><p>The Bears don’t have to turn in their first injury report until Thursday afternoon and don’t have to set their Monday night roster until earlier that afternoon.</p>

entries.title: Mayor Johnson's top lawyer will step down, UIC law professor poised to step into the job
entries.summary: <p>Mayor Brandon Johnson is losing a top official who became a pillar in the city’s first line of defense against the Trump administration while holding one of the most sensitive and trusted positions in city government.</p><p>Mary Richardson-Lowry is stepping down from her role as the city’s corporation counsel after more than three years, Johnson told WBEZ. She is the latest and one of the last remaining original appointees to leave Johnson’s administration.</p><p></p><p>Richardson-Lowry, a seasoned attorney who came out of retirement to become the first Black woman to fill the role, will be replaced by Renee Hatcher, a career academic who is an assistant clinical law professor and legal clinic director at the University of Illinois-Chicago. Her appointment requires City Council approval.</p><p>Johnson rebuffed the idea that the change in leadership comes at an inopportune time, as the city juggles numerous high stakes legal battles and Johnson embarks on an <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/elections/2026/09/13/chicago-mayor-brandon-johnson-announcement-reelection-bid-2027" >uphill battle for reelection.</a></p><p>“This is the appropriate time to transition,” Johnson said in an interview. “As I prepare for a second term, [I’m] sending a real clear message to working people in this city that our work has just begun.”</p><p>In an interview with the Chicago Sun-Times, Richardson-Lowry said she’s not leaving because she’s afraid that Johnson will lose the election. She simply wants to go home.</p><p>“I de-camped back to Chicago to serve from Arizona. I left my husband and dogs behind to meet my service requirements. And it has come to a close,” she said.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-c10000" name="image-c10000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/999da0c/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6833x3835+0+360/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F3c%2F3f%2F16d0898741928c6aacab9fa8dc76%2Fwatts-091225-7.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/d5bcc8b/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6833x3835+0+360/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F3c%2F3f%2F16d0898741928c6aacab9fa8dc76%2Fwatts-091225-7.jpg 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/a622ff4/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6833x3835+0+360/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F3c%2F3f%2F16d0898741928c6aacab9fa8dc76%2Fwatts-091225-7.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="ity of Chicago Corporation Counsel Mary B. Richardson-Lowry speaks during a news conference at 2 N. Ronald Watts and his tactical team members.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Pat Nabong/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>With Hatcher’s appointment, Johnson is also recasting the Law Department’s priorities, he said. The department is tasked with everything from defending police officers against misconduct lawsuits, to negotiating development contracts, to advising the mayor at City Council meetings.</p><p>But Johnson said he wants to see more affirmative litigation — a legal approach of proactively going after bad actors to protect consumers and residents from abuse. That’s largely how the Illinois attorney general operates.</p><p>“We have to be far more aggressive in protecting working people” because of the rise of “right-wing extremism,” he said.</p><p>“We've had to maintain a defensive posture in this season because of the federal overreach. But my vision going into my second term is to improve the quality of life for everyday people and to use the tools available to me… As affordability continues to be a challenge for Chicagoans and people across the globe, having a Department of Law that is aggressively thinking about how we can be more affirmative in our approach to provide economic justice for people.”</p><p>Johnson and Richardson-Lowry had already begun this approach. The mayor’s 2026 budget proposal grew the department’s affirmative litigation division by $530,000 and added five employees.</p><p>And the city sued Glock, Inc. in an attempt to hold the gun manufacturer accountable for selling pistols that can be converted into automatic weapons. Richardson-Lowry has also led or joined roughly 80 lawsuits against the Trump administration to stave off threats to cut hundreds of millions of dollars in federal funding.</p><p>Hatcher is the daughter of civil rights advocate and first Black mayor of Gary, Indiana, Richard Hatcher, who led that city for 20 years.</p><p>She has directed UIC’s Community Enterprise & Solidarity Economy Clinic for nearly a decade, overseeing student legal representation of worker-owned businesses, non-profits and small businesses that operate “for the benefit of an underserved community.”</p><p>Hatcher received her law degree from New York University. Before her clinic role, she held fellowships at the University of Baltimore and the Institute for Urban Policy Research & Analysis at the University of Texas. She worked as a staff attorney for the Chicago Lawyers’ Committee for Civil Rights for three years early in her career.</p><p>She steps into the role without any formal government experience.</p><p>But she told WBEZ she is “more than prepared” to lead Chicago’s $47.9 million Law Department and its roughly 330 employees.</p><p>“I don't have the profile of a typical corporation counsel, but I actually think that's a positive in this case — it's not to say that I don't understand how this works. I'm happy to answer any criticism with how I actually show up and do the job,” she said.</p><p>“My career has been committed to public interest law. I have tried to use lawyering as a means to improve communities and neighborhoods,” she said.</p><p></p><p>City attorneys are currently defending two of Johnson’s newly created revenue streams: a tax on social media companies and a licensing scheme for online sports betting. The city is also, with the state of Illinois, suing the Trump administration over Operation Midway Blitz. That’s on top of hashing out a major forthcoming global settlement for survivors of police torture.</p><p>Johnson called Hatcher a “quick study” and noted that Richardson-Lowry is “passing the torch” to who would be the second Black woman to hold the role.</p><p>But any mentorship would likely happen off-the-clock, as the formal overlap between the two on city payrolls will be almost non-existent. Richardson-Lowry’s last day is Oct. 1, the day Hatcher starts as interim corporation counsel.</p><p></p><p>Richardson-Lowry has fiercely defended Johnson and his policies since accepting the role in June 2023.</p><p>She publicly sparred with the city’s former Inspector General over access to investigate the mayor’s office. She sat behind Johnson through hours of testimony as he defended Chicago’s sanctuary city laws at a divisive and highly <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/brandonjohnson/2025/03/05/chicago-sanctuary-city-brandon-johnson-testimony-updates-file" >politicized Congressional hearing</a> in 2025.</p><div class="Enhancement" entries.title: Bears claim long snapper Scott Daly off Saints practice squad
entries.summary: <p>The <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Bears</a> brought back long snapper Scott Daly after rookie Beau Gardner struggled through his first two games.</p><p>They claimed him from the Saints practice squad Tuesday, cutting Gardner.</p><p> Daly played on the team's active roster Sunday.</p><p>Daly returns to the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/halas-intrigue/2026/09/20/bears-vikings-podcast-caleb-williams-halas-intrigue" target="_blank" >Bears</a> after playing all 34 regular-season games for them from 2024-25. They let him leave via free agency in the spring, choosing to rely on two young options during training camp. The Notre Dame alum signed with the Buccaneers, who cut him Aug. 31. He spent two weeks with the Packers before joining the Saints.</p><p>Daly, who went to Downers Grove South High School, will reunite with kicker Cairo Santos and punter Tory Taylor. The trio proved successful during their two years together.</p><p>Coach Ben Johnson hinted that he'd make a change at long snapper on Monday, one day after a high snap from Gardner led to the Vikings blocking a potential game-tying field goal late in the fourth quarter.</p><p>The Bears also signed cornerback Nick McCloud, who also played for them last year, to the practice squad after Tyrique Stevenson hurt his hamstring. Practice squad offensive lineman Kyle Hergel was cut. </p>

entries.title: Art Institute of Chicago to return looted Holocaust-era painting to family of persecuted art collector
entries.summary: <p>The Art Institute of Chicago is returning the Cubist painting “Woman with a Fan” by French artist Jean Metzinger to the Lewenstein family, the institution announced Tuesday.</p><p>The oil painting from 1913 was lost during a forced Nazi-era sale in the Netherlands. However, there were significant gaps in the painting’s historical record, said Jacques Schuhmacher, the museum’s executive director of provenance.</p><p>The work resurfaced on the Dutch art market in the 1950s, moved through galleries in Paris and New York City, and was later acquired by the Art Institute of Chicago in 1959, when Mr. and Mrs. Sigmund Kunstadter donated the work to the Chicago museum.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-2c0000" name="image-2c0000"></a> <picture 1959.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>© 2026 Artists Rights Society (ARS), New York / ADAGP, Paris</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>But through modern infrared imaging technology, Schuhmacher said, researchers discovered a name written in faint pencil on the back of the piece: Paul Citroen. Citroen was a Dutch art dealer in Berlin and the Netherlands who sold the work to art collector Emmanuel Lewenstein.</p><p>“This allowed us to make a connection between our painting and the Lewenstein family for the first time,” Schuhmacher said. “With the evidence written on the painting itself, we carried out additional research in collaboration with the Mondex Corporation.”</p><p>Industrywide, artistic provenance has become a key focus of museum leaders and has been the subject of complex court cases and legal disputes. In 2024, the Art Institute <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/art/2024/12/02/art-institute-chicago-provenance-team-jacques-schuhmacher-nazi-matisse-daisies-egon-schiele-gustave-courbet" target="_blank" >announced the appointment</a> of Schuhmacher as its first executive director of provenance research and operates one of the largest such departments in the country.</p><p>Last week, a New York City appellate court ruled that a different World War II-era painting, a 1916 watercolor and pencil drawing by Egon Schiele titled “Russian War Prisoner,” <a class="Link" href="https://www.nytimes.com/2026/09/18/arts/egon-schiele-chicago-museum-appellate-court-ruling.html" target="_blank" ><u>could remain at the Art Institute of Chicago</u></a> while ownership disputes are handled in civil court.</p><p>Investigators for the Manhattan district attorney’s office cited a penal law that governs the disposal of stolen property. And in 2025, a New York Supreme Court judge <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/museums/2025/04/24/art-institute-of-chicago-egon-schiele-russian-war-prisoner-nazi-stolen-art" target="_blank" ><u>determined that the Schiele had been stolen by Nazis from Fritz Grünbaum before the start of World War II</u></a>. Two years prior, authorities officially approved the seizure of the artwork from the Art Institute in 2023, but let it stay at the museum.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-hangRight> <div Brackstone Solow from Dr. Eugene A. Solow and Family/Art Institute of Chicago</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>The Art Institute maintains that it purchased “Russian War Prisoner” legally in 1966, and in a statement said that the Metzinger and Schiele works are two very different cases.</p><p>“We are confident in our extensive research, which indicates very different facts for each of the two works,” the statement reads. “Evidence indicates the Metzinger painting was seized from the family and forcibly sold, while evidence related to the Schiele drawing indicates it was never seized, stayed within the family, and was ultimately sold by the family more than ten years after the war.”</p><p>In the case of “Woman with a Fan,” Lewenstein’s heirs are represented by the Toronto-based firm, which specializes in the recovery of art and cultural artifacts that were looted or stolen during the Holocaust.</p><p>“In provenance research you often triangulate different kinds of sources,” <br>Schuhmacher said. “Taken together, [we] confirmed that our painting was sold as a result of Nazi persecution in 1940 in the Netherlands.”</p><p>But with the new discovery, the case required a close look at archives from the Netherlands. “We found documents from Paul Citroen, which showed that he sold this painting to Emanuel Lewenstein in 1928,” Schuhmacher said.</p><p>Years later, in 1933, Adolf Hitler became the chancellor of Germany, which marked the effective seizure of power by the Nazi Party. By 1940, World War II was in full effect and the Nazis had occupied the Netherlands, where the Lewenstein family lived.</p><p>“The Lewensteins were Jewish. They were persecuted because they were Jewish,” Schuhmacher said.</p><p>With the uncovered documents, which included an auction catalog from 1940 and a Dutch newspaper article from the same year, researchers were able to verify the exact dimensions of the Metzinger painting and match it with the one in the Art Institute’s collection. They determined then that the painting should go back to the Lewenstein family.</p><p>“The decision was made to restitute [the painting] to the Lewenstein heirs, and I think what's really important here is that in restituting a piece, it's not just about transferring ownership back to a family,” Schumacher said. “It's also about restoring the agency [to the family] to do with this painting what they think is appropriate.”</p><p>Megan Michienzi, spokesperson for the Art Institute of Chicago, confirmed that the Metzinger painting is no longer on view at the museum. The museum is working with art handlers to arrange for the work to be sent back to the living heirs of the late art collector, Michienzi said.</p><p>Michienzi said the Art Institute has “prioritized provenance research, and we are happy to return items when we learn new information that suggests that they should go back.”</p>

entries.title: How Bowen Byram's innate confidence helps him play his style, handle pressure with Blackhawks
entries.summary: <p>There is enormous pressure on new <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/blackhawks" target="_blank" >Blackhawks</a> No. 1 defenseman Bowen Byram to justify the assets the team relinquished to acquire him and live up to the six-year, $75 million contract they gave him.</p><p>Former No. 1 defenseman Seth Jones faced similarly enormous pressure and never seemed to fully get out from under it.</p><p>But the Hawks have reason to believe Byram can. He possesses an innate, unshakable self-belief that he can be a stellar No. 1 defenseman and that he is worth <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/blackhawks/2026/07/01/blackhawks-bowen-byram-contract-nhl-defensemen-free-agency" >$75 million</a>.</p><p>"There’s a swagger about him that he carries with himself," Alex Vlasic said. "It’s never cockiness, but it’s quiet confidence. That’s something I'm trying to pick up on, as well.</p><p>"I think any of the good players in the league have that type of swagger. You need it to — if you make a mistake — move on from it and know you’re going to make a nice play right after. He definitely has that about him. It’s a pretty unique factor."</p><p>That confidence is evident in Byram’s on-ice play, too. He demonstrated it throughout his impressive Hawks preseason debut Monday, during which he recorded three goals and five shots in over 23 minutes of ice time.</p><p>Offensively, he jumped up into rushes or pinched down into the offensive zone at the right times. </p><p>His first goal showcased his accurate shooting, his second showcased his vision and savvy passing (which led to a lucky bounce) and his third showcased his ability to protect the puck while moving at speed.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" > <div class="TweetUrl"> <blockquote class="twitter-tweet"><p lang="en" dir="ltr">GOAL: Bowen Byram picks the top corner with a shot from the right circle. <a href="https://t.co/e34Zy6eGiW">pic.twitter.com/e34Zy6eGiW</a></p>— BHF (@BlackhawksFocus) <a href="https://x.com/BlackhawksFocus/status/2102201627792884150?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">September 22, 2026</a></blockquote> <script async src="https://platform.x.com/widgets.js" charset="utf-8"></script> </div> </div> </div></div><p>And defensively, he displayed how he can use his exceptional quickness and agility to get back into position in a blink even after small bobbles or mistakes. </p><p>That, in turn, allows him to play more fluidly since he doesn’t need to worry much about small bobbles or mistakes.</p><p>"I just trust my feet," Byram said. "If I feel like I can make a play or get to a puck, I'm going to trust my instincts. If it doesn't work out, I'll work my butt off to get back."</p><p>He managed to exhibit all of that even after a disastrous first 15 seconds, during which he turned the puck over behind the net, lost his man and allowed a goal against.</p><p>That ideally won’t happen often during the regular season, but his bounce-back in this case did exemplify his mental resilience.</p><p>"I was having some weird thoughts in my head after that," he said. "I was like, 'This is really how it's going to start, eh?' At the start of the game, I was pretty nervous, to be honest. But once I got a few shifts in, I settled down and just focused on trying to play quick and get in the rush and defend hard."</p><p>The Hawks hope Byram can elevate their defense not only through his own play but also by helping everyone else. </p><p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/blackhawks/2026/08/23/blackhawks-alex-vlasic-playoffs-louis-crevier-bowen-byram-patrick-kane" >Vlasic</a>, who has somewhat plateaued since his 2023-24 breakout season, looks like a perfect fit as Byram's partner, and it’s easy to imagine their pairing thriving this season. </p><p>Vlasic read Byram’s aggressive moves and, using his long reach and stick-on-puck skills, effectively covered for him Monday as the more conservative half of the pairing.</p><p>"We want [Vlasic] to become a great stopper in this league," coach Jeff Blashill said. "You don't have to be...in like a shutdown pair. You can be a great stopper and play with a puck-moving defenseman and have a lot of complementary strengths for each other."</p><p>One interesting question: Can Byram’s unshakable self-belief rub off on his teammates? Some Hawks could use more of that. </p><p>Young defenseman Sam Rinzel, for one, thinks it could.</p><p>"Everything is between the ears," Rinzel said. "You can have the best ability in the world, but if you don't have that belief... With us being so young, if we believe, it'll be just fine."</p>

entries.title: Review: If music is the food of love, then Chicago Shakes’ buoyant ‘Play On’ is a feast
entries.summary: <p>It’s a dangerous gambit to tell an audience they’re about to experience something great. Set people’s expectations high, and it’s that much harder to meet them.</p><p>So in “Play On!,” the musical based on the music of Duke Ellington and now running through Oct. 18 at the Chicago Shakespeare Theater, when two characters talk about how much they love the song “Mood Indigo” before it is performed, you think, “I am ready for something great.” If you happen to be a reviewer, especially one who also loves the song “Mood Indigo,” you think, “OK, this is what they want to be judged on.”</p><p>Reader, it was something great. Krystal Joy Brown, who portrays nightclub singer Lady Liv, delivered a time-stopping rendition of the song, with gorgeous sorrowful phrasing and effortless navigation of the melody’s tricky accidentals. The theater was utterly still, rapt, and there was a collective sense of remembering to breathe again during the applause.</p><div class="RatingCard Enhancement" data-module data-rating="4.0" data-align-center> <div class="RatingCard-title"> ‘Play On’ </div> <div class="RatingCard-content"> <span class="RatingCard-star"> <span class="RatingCard-star-full"> <svg class=""> <use xlink:href="#icon-star"></use> </svg> </span> <span class="RatingCard-star-half"> <svg class=""> <use xlink:href="#icon-star"></use> </svg> </span> </span> <span class="RatingCard-star"> <span class="RatingCard-star-full"> <svg class=""> <use xlink:href="#icon-star"></use> </svg> </span> <span class="RatingCard-star-half"> <svg class=""> <use xlink:href="#icon-star"></use> </svg> </span> </span> <span class="RatingCard-star"> <span class="RatingCard-star-full"> <svg class=""> <use xlink:href="#icon-star"></use> </svg> </span> <span class="RatingCard-star-half"> <svg class=""> <use xlink:href="#icon-star"></use> </svg> </span> </span> <span class="RatingCard-star"> <span class="RatingCard-star-full"> <svg class=""> <use xlink:href="#icon-star"></use> </svg> </span> <span class="RatingCard-star-half"> <svg class=""> <use xlink:href="#icon-star"></use> </svg> </span> </span> </div> </div><p></p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-b30000" name="module-b30000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><b>When:</b> Through Oct. 18<br><b>Where:</b> Chicago Shakespeare Theater, 800 E. Grand Ave.<br><b>Tickets:</b> $55–$135<br><b>Information:</b> <a class="Link" href="https://www.chicagoshakes.com/productions/2627-play-on/" target="_blank" >chicagoshakes.com</a><br><b>Run time:</b> 2 hours, 30 minutes, including an intermission</div> </div><p>“Mood Indigo” in miniature matched “Play On!” as a whole. The show took some of the most magnificent music ever written by an American composer, filtered it through a classic Shakespeare comedy and produced a first-rate show that does justice to both.</p><p>“Play On!,” conceived by Sheldon Epps, who directs this revival, borrows the scaffolding of its plot from “Twelfth Night.” The story opens with Vy (Hailee Kaleem Wright), an aspiring songwriter, arriving at the scene of the action, except instead of being shipwrecked like Viola from Shakespeare’s play, she takes the A train to Harlem. She hopes to meet Duke Ellington (Edred Utomi) — analogue of Duke Orsino — but learns that songwriting is a man’s world. She dresses as a man and lands an introduction to Duke under the unlikely name of Vy-Man.</p><p>She/he finds Duke forlorn, pining for Lady Liv and suffering from writer’s block. They work on one of Vy’s songs, which is “Don’t Get Around Much Anymore,” and Vy agrees to take it to Lady Liv like a love letter, claiming it is Duke’s own work.</p><p>By the rules of Shakespearean farce, Lady Liv falls in love with Vy-Man, while Vy is smitten with Duke, outlining the love triangle. Duke, while wooing Lady Liv remotely, becomes confused about his feelings for Vy-Man, and an uptight assistant named Rev (Alan H Green) provides a fourth vertex such that the happily-ever-afters can be tidily paired up.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-8f0000" name="image-8f0000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/8794264/2147483647/strip/true/crop/7495x4206+0+396/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F99%2Fb1%2Ff5357c164738ac4cd8592f1c6412%2F4-cst-playon-press-photo-by-kyle-flubacker.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/d4d2a5f/2147483647/strip/true/crop/7495x4206+0+396/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F99%2Fb1%2Ff5357c164738ac4cd8592f1c6412%2F4-cst-playon-press-photo-by-kyle-flubacker.jpg 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/4ddf013/2147483647/strip/true/crop/7495x4206+0+396/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F99%2Fb1%2Ff5357c164738ac4cd8592f1c6412%2F4-cst-playon-press-photo-by-kyle-flubacker.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="Krystal Joy Brown as Lady Liv in Chicago Shakespeare’s production of Play On! Conceived and directed by Sheldon Epps, the production runs September 11 -October 18, 2026, in The Yard at Chicago Shakespeare." srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/4ddf013/2147483647/strip/true/crop/7495x4206+0+396/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F99%2Fb1%2Ff5357c164738ac4cd8592f1c6412%2F4-cst-playon-press-photo-by-kyle-flubacker.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/26367b3/2147483647/strip/true/crop/7495x4206+0+396/resize/980x550!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F99%2Fb1%2Ff5357c164738ac4cd8592f1c6412%2F4-cst-playon-press-photo-by-kyle-flubacker.jpg 2x" width="490" height="275" data-src="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/4ddf013/2147483647/strip/true/crop/7495x4206+0+396/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F99%2Fb1%2Ff5357c164738ac4cd8592f1c6412%2F4-cst-playon-press-photo-by-kyle-flubacker.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" > </picture> <div class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Krystal Joy Brown stars as Lady Liv in Chicago Shakespeare’s production of “Play On!”</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Kyle Flubacker</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Throughout, the cast sprinkles in the songs of the real-life Duke Ellington, including — in addition to those already mentioned — “I’m Beginning to See the Light,” “Prelude to a Kiss” and “It Don’t Mean a Thing (If It Ain’t Got That Swing).” The quartet singing “Solitude” at the close of the first half nailed some gnarly jazz harmonies. Brown stopped the show a second time after intermission with “I Ain’t Got Nothin’ But the Blues.”</p><p>And therein the show shines. The level of musicianship among the cast is almost impossibly high, with all the principals capable of solo turns but ready for tight harmony (the trio singing the doo-wats on “It Don’t Mean a Thing” also deserve a shoutout), and the ensemble does it all while dancing. The six-piece combo accompanying the show hit all their marks at this past Saturday’s matinee under the direction of Nathanael Wilkerson, filling in for music director Theodis Rodgers Jr., the regular conductor.</p><p>The jukebox-musical format of building a show around pre-existing tunes has several built-in flaws, all of which “Play On!” either covers over or skirts impressively. The foremost innate problem is that for pop-music jukebox musicals, the familiar songs will not sound exactly like their familiar recordings. But jazz already works by making every performance unique, through improvised solos and bandleaders’ different takes and orchestrations.</p><p>The other biggest jukebox-musical flaw is the difficulty of shoehorning in songs that audiences expect to hear but don’t fit into the story. Here, having songwriters and a singer as main characters allows some songs to be slotted in irrespective of the narrative, but also Duke Ellington’s catalog contains a lot of lovelorn ballads befitting a tale of many unrequited loves, as the characters observe within the show, in a moment that doesn’t exactly break the fourth wall but does kind of tap on it.</p><div class="Enhancement" Shakespeare buffs will recognize several allusions to famous lines from “Twelfth Night.” Probably you already spotted the one in the title, about music as the food of love. In that vein, “Play On!” is quite a banquet.</p>

entries.title: Gov. JB Pritzker assembling Illinois Artificial Intelligence Cabinet to assess AI threats
entries.summary: <p>Gov. JB Pritzker is convening a panel of experts to advise state officials on the potential threats of artificial intelligence as a growing number of industry leaders warn the burgeoning, self-improving technology could spell doomsday for humanity if left unchecked.</p><p>The Democratic governor signed an executive order Tuesday establishing the Illinois Artificial Intelligence Cabinet to assess “the various risks posed by Al to the safety of Illinois residents and the critical infrastructure residents rely on.”</p><p>Pritzker will name his AI Cabinet members “in the coming weeks” to work alongside numerous state agency leaders, including from the Department of Innovation and Technology, the Department of Public Health and the Illinois Emergency Management Agency.</p><p>They’re expected to come from backgrounds in academia, law, ethics and governance, and provide recommendations on potential public safety threats, protecting public assets and evaluating possible regulations, according to Pritzker’s office.</p><p>His order comes in the wake of former Anthropic AI researcher Jacob Coxon’s media blitz this month warning that aggressive industry development in the absence of federal regulation “could kill us all by the end of the decade.”</p><p>OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, Meta chairman Mark Zuckerberg and other AI executives have emphasized the need for broader safety measures.</p><p>“Artificial Intelligence has enormous potential to transform our everyday lives, but when experts and industry leaders sound the alarm bell, urge us to slow down, and ask for guardrails, we should listen,” Pritzker said in a statement.</p><p>In July, Pritzker signed <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/politics/2026/07/06/ai-regulations-illinois-law-pritzker-signed" target="_blank" ><u>a package of state-level AI regulations into law</u></a> that mark some of the most stringent in the nation, requiring frontier developers to submit to annual independent audits.</p><p>Companies also have to publish safety plans explaining how they’ll mitigate “catastrophic risk” from their platforms, including anything that could “contribute to the death of, or serious injury to, more than 50 people,” by supplying “expert-level assistance in the creation or release of a chemical, biological, radiological or nuclear weapon,” the law states.</p><p>It all comes as a host of potential 2028 presidential contenders seek to position themselves as thoughtful authorities on technology that’s weaving its way into everyday life, whether Americans like it or not.</p><p>Pritzker, who has done little to quell speculation about his own presidential ambitions, has blasted President Donald Trump for his administration’s lax approach to AI regulation.</p><p>“Illinois has already enacted nation-leading laws that hold Big Tech accountable and today I’m taking executive action to keep this a priority,” Pritzker said. “Congress and the White House need to treat AI risks with urgency, but in the meantime, Illinois won’t wait because it is our foremost responsibility to prepare and protect Illinoisans.”</p><p>University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign Chancellor Charles Isbell said in a statement that his institution is “eager to help the state navigate the current challenges and opportunities that AI brings.”</p><p>“As a land-grant institution, we are committed to innovation for the public good and to developing human-centered AI that protects privacy, reduces bias, strengthens democratic institutions, uses energy wisely, and creates value for workers, companies and communities,” Isbell said.</p>
entries.author: Mitchell Armentrout

entries.title: Mayoral hopeful Bill Quinlan sues in bid to shrink field of candidates
entries.summary: <p>Illinois Secretary of State Alexi Giannoulias and three other mayoral challengers have been accused of trying to have it both ways by running for re-election while simultaneously <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/elections/2026/09/13/who-is-running-for-chicago-mayor-2027-election" >running for mayor.</a></p><p>Attorney <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/elections/2026/09/15/william-j-quinlan-candidate-chicago-mayoral-race-2027-son-richard-j-daley-corporation-counsel" >William J. Quinlan</a> is now trying to turn that political argument into a legal one that, if successful, could shrink by four the field of candidates seeking to deny Mayor Brandon Johnson a second term.</p><p>An election law expert, Quinlan filed a lawsuit Tuesday in Cook County Circuit Court asking a judge to uphold a revised Illinois election law that includes an expedited filing calendar for mayoral candidates.</p><p>If Quinlan succeeds, Giannoulias, U.S. Rep. Mike Quigley (D-Il.), Cook County Treasurer Maria Pappas and Board of Review Commissioner George Cardenas would be forced to make a choice. They could either seek re-election to their current offices or file nominating petitions for mayor. If they tried to do both, they would risk being thrown off the ballot for both offices — if Quinlan wins the case.</p><p>Chicago has a long history of politicians who have run for two offices at once without being forced to choose between the two. At most, they faced a few political potshots from opponents. But that was before the election calendar was changed.</p><p>Mayoral candidates now must file their nominating petitions by Oct. 26. That’s eight days before the Nov. 3 election. According to Quinlan, that “changes everything.”</p><p>“The law says you cannot file two sets of petitions... at the same time for incompatible offices. If you do, you have to withdraw from one of the offices within five days after filing them. If you don’t, you’re disqualified from both,” Quinlan said.</p><p>An election law expert who asked to remain anonymous dismissed Quinlan’s lawsuit as a legal longshot. The expert said that the law simply prohibits candidates from filing nominating petitions for more than one office on the ballot in the same election. It does not preclude candidates from filing nominating petitions for offices in two different elections.</p><p>Cardenas agreed. “Other elected officials have done this pattern quite successfully many times,” the former alderperson said. “It sounds to me more of a desperate move by Quinlan. He gets in at the last minute and wants to clear the field. I don’t think he’s got a shot." </p><p>Giannoulias, the presumed frontrunner with a campaign war chest of $22 million, did not respond to the lawsuit, instead releasing a statement: “Alexi is focused on talking to Chicagoans about the issues they care about: making Chicago a safer, more affordable place to live.” </p><p>Quigley dismissed the lawsuit as a publicity stunt by a candidate who “nobody knows, doesn’t have a base and will be lucky to get on the ballot.”</p><p>“The guy who was general counsel to [former Illinois Gov. Rod ] Blagojevich is going to tell us how we should operate in our lives?” Quigley said of the now-convicted former governor.</p><p>Pappas said she has not formally announced her candidacy for mayor, so the suit shouldn't apply to her. </p><p></p><p></p><p></p><p> Quinlan served as an election attorney for leading Democrats, including in the 2012 reelection campaign of then-President Barack Obama, and as an attorney for fired former Chicago Public Schools CEO Pedro Martinez. He denied that the lawsuit is a publicity stunt aimed at raising his political profile. </p><p></p><p>“The result of this is that you’re going to have a Republican secretary of state, a Republican congressman and, potentially a Republican treasurer because if they run for both as they say they’re going to, they will be disqualified from staying on the ballot and the person on the other side will win,” Quinlan said.</p><p></p><p>The lawsuit seeks a declaratory judgment in Quinlan's favor and an expedited hearing to resolve the issue well before the Nov. 3 election, when all four of the challengers he is targeting are seeking re-election to the offices they now hold.</p>
entries.author: Fran Spielman

entries.title: Cooked without Caleb? Remember, Bears beat — no, dominated — Eagles last year despite Williams' worst outing
entries.summary: <p>Three things I think I know about the now-you-see-them, now-you-don’t <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Bears</a>, who are 1-1 after an offensive disappearing act in a <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/09/20/caleb-williams-hurt-bears-vikings-soldier-field-nfl" target="_blank" >costly 9-3 loss to the Vikings</a>:</p><p><b>1. They can’t rush Caleb Williams: </b>Even if the star quarterback swears on a stack of playbooks that <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/09/21/bears-qb-caleb-williams-hamstring-avoided-serious-hamstring-injury-mri" target="_blank" >his strained right hamstring</a> shouldn’t stop the team from sending him out there Monday night against the Eagles at Soldier Field, the Bears should duct-tape a clipboard to his hands and shroud him in bubble wrap until October 4 against the Jets at the soonest.</p><p>It’s probably a long shot that Williams will face the Eagles as it is, but the Bears ought to err on the side of caution even if it means starting backup Tyson Bagent against the Jets, too. (Assuming Bagent <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/09/22/bears-qb-tyson-bagent-concussion-case-keenum" >makes it out of concussion protocol</a>.) If Williams is capable of playing the position well without fiendish scrambles and mad dashes for first downs and touchdowns, we’ve yet to see it. Is a relegated-to-the-pocket Williams any better than the next guy, in this case $5 million-a-year Bagent? Not sure why he would be. Bagent has command of the offense and — just saying — working legs to go with it. You paid the man, so play the man.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" > <div class="TweetUrl"> <blockquote class="twitter-tweet"><p lang="zxx" dir="ltr"><a href="https://t.co/uybKUhbx13">pic.twitter.com/uybKUhbx13</a></p>— Patrick Finley (@patrickfinley) <a href="https://x.com/patrickfinley/status/2101774656466206977?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">September 20, 2026</a></blockquote> <script async src="https://platform.x.com/widgets.js" charset="utf-8"></script> </div> </div> </div></div><p><b>2. They have to rush the football: </b>Look no further than last year’s game against the Eagles — a 24-15 upset the day after Thanksgiving — for an example of what a running game can do for a team.</p><p>D’Andre Swift carried 18 times for 125 yards. Kyle Monangai toted it 22 times for 130. It was the first time in 40 years — since Walter Payton and Matt Suhey in 1985, the Super Bowl season — the Bears had two 100-yard rushers in a game. The Bears doubled the Eagles in first downs and came within a few ticks of doubling them in time of possession. Coach Ben Johnson famously tore off his shirt. The Bears had a fifth win in a row and were 9-3, alone in first in the NFC North.</p><p>It happened despite Williams’ lowest completion percentage (47.2%), passing yards (154) and passer rating (56.9) of 2025 — Johnson admitted afterward he’d called too many passing plays (37) — and yet it was as good a win, and as good as the Bears felt after a win, all season. That’s a timely lesson on which to hark back.</p><p><b>3. They have to take turns: </b>Of all the turnovers created last season by the Bears, the biggest might have been Nahshon Wright’s cagey, brilliant yank-out of the ball from Eagles QB Jalen Hurts on a “tush push” sneak in the red zone. Wright isn’t a Bear anymore, but the echoes of a team that created the most turnovers in the league and committed the fewest remain.</p><p>After Swift’s crushing fumble at the 1-yard line against the Vikings — who won the turnover battle 2-0 — the Bears have to rediscover this critical part of their identity. Without it, they might not be anything special.</p><h3><b>Look who’s coming: the Eagles</b></h3><p>They’re 2-0, which sounds great if you’re the Bears and taking them in from a 1-1 point of view, but they haven’t looked like one of the league’s top teams yet. Might that change? Sure. So far, though, they’re a middle-of-the-pack team offensively as well as when it comes to defending against the run. That might make them the type of opponent the Bears are looking for.</p><p>In particular, the Eagles are concerned about their offensive line. The offense had a mere 10 first downs in an opening win against the Commanders, and Hurts ran for his life for much of a 24-20 win at the Titans in Week 2. One would like to think the Bears are better than either of the Eagles’ opponents to date.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-ab0000" name="image-ab0000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/c95a51e/2147483647/strip/true/crop/5109x2867+0+269/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F81%2Fe5%2F0f8b3b2c4b3babb8e579df878886%2Fvikings-bears-football-3.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/eede74d/2147483647/strip/true/crop/5109x2867+0+269/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F81%2Fe5%2F0f8b3b2c4b3babb8e579df878886%2Fvikings-bears-football-3.jpg 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/36b02d4/2147483647/strip/true/crop/5109x2867+0+269/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F81%2Fe5%2F0f8b3b2c4b3babb8e579df878886%2Fvikings-bears-football-3.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="Bears head coach Ben Johnson walks off the field after the Bears lost to the Minnesota Vikings at Soldier Field on Sunday, Sept. 20, 2026. Huh/AP </p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p></p><h3><b>Ben-o-meter: 5 out of 10</b></h3><p>Johnson’s offense ran wild in a 59-point game at Carolina to start the season. Hello, genius.</p><p>Next came the mother of all tail-kickings by defensive coordinator Brian Flores and the Vikings. Hello, fraud.</p><p>So which is it? Genius or fraud? Neither, of course. Let’s not be too reactionary here.</p><p>But with the Bears coming off a game in which their offense bumbled and crumbled, it’s fair and reasonable to hold Johnson to account and expect him to respond with a good week. In the NFL, reputations are fleeting.</p><h3><b>Take the North</b></h3><p>Heading into the season, oddsmakers had the Vikings as the worst team in the division. Now, the Vikings are the betting favorite. See? Fleeting.</p><p>By the way, the Bears currently are the longest shot to win the North. So they’ve got that going for them.</p><h3><b>Three and Out</b></h3><p><b>1. We’ll take the hammy, we think.</p><p><b>3. Is it Monday yet? </b>The sooner the Bears get the stink of Sunday’s debacle off them, the better. entries.title: Sky veteran Rachel Banham is starting to think about life after basketball
entries.summary: <p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/chicago-sky" target="_blank" >Sky</a> guard Rachel Banham is starting to get ready for the next chapter of her life. Not right at this very moment — she thinks she’s got another year, maybe two, of playing in her — but her body and mind are telling her a transition is coming.</p><p>“Every year you can feel it get a little closer,” she told the Sun-Times before the Sky’s last home game of the season.</p><p>Though imagining life without playing basketball feels weird, she already has an inkling of what it may look like. For starters: She wants to have kids. All her friends have them now, and she’s always loved them.</p><p>And secondly: she wants to coach in the league.</p><p>She got her feet wet as an assistant coach at her alma mater, the University of Minnesota, from 2022-2024. But she’s known pretty much throughout her playing career that coaching was in her future. From the time she entered the W, she found herself sitting in on staff meetings, thinking about the game from a higher level.</p><p>“Film has always fascinated me,” she said. “I love watching basketball. Like a gross amount. It’s just something that I always am thinking about.”</p><p>Banham has been lucky to have some good teachers. She was drafted No. 4 to the Sun in 2016, played for the Lynx from 2020-23 and then returned to the Sun before ultimately getting traded to Chicago.</p><p>As a result, she’s seen some of the best coaches in the WNBA at work: Curt Miller in Connecticut, Cheryl Reeve in Minnesota and Stephanie White the second time around with the Sun.</p><p>All great coaches have virtues they try to embody for their teams. Accountability is the one that most calls to Banham. She was impressed by how well Reeve modeled it, relentlessly pushing her teams to their potential. Once Banham has her own squad, she wants to be “kind of annoying,” in that same way.</p><p>“I’m gonna be like: We’re gonna do it right, and if you do it wrong, we’re doing it again.”</p><p>Sky coach Tyler Marsh has already witnessed Banham model that trait in the two years they’ve been together. To outsiders, she may seem like a goofball — and there’s no doubt she is — but to Marsh, it’s her businesslike approach that’s kept her in the league for more than a decade.</p><p>Last season with the Sky, she made the best of a <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/chicago-sky/2025/07/31/rachel-banham-brings-the-weird-out-of-her-teammates-while-adapts-to-point-guard-role" >rough situation</a>. After point guard Courtney Vandersloot went down with an ACL tear, Banham stepped into the largest role of her career, starting at point guard and averaging a career-high nine points.</p><p>This season, her role diminished. She started the season in a shooting slump and ended up playing fewer than 15 minutes per game.</p><p>But what impresses Marsh is that her approach didn’t change at all. Which isn’t to say Banham hasn’t gotten frustrated.</p><p>The Sky once again missed the playoffs, and Banham never fully found her stroke, shooting her lowest percentage in years.</p><p>“It’s been a really hard season, to be honest,” Banham said. “As much as this stuff sucks, I try to take it as a lesson. I’m learning so many lessons about how I want to coach, how I want to be as a player the following season, how I want to be as a person, and how I approach each day.”</p><p>As one of three veterans headed for free agency, Banham and the Sky must also decide what’s next. She has been a key culture piece, as they call it in the business. But with nine players under contract for next season and two first-round picks in the 2027 draft, only a few roster spots will be available.</p><p>Decisions for another day.</p><p>In the meantime, Banham is looking forward to an offseason gig as a Big Ten Network studio analyst and color commentator.</p><p>A perfect bridge to the next chapter, a great opportunity to put her “gross” amount of film-watching to good use.</p>

entries.title: Cubs get ‘great news’ on Alex Bregman, who won’t go on injured list, could return before regular season ends
entries.summary: <p>Watching Alex Bregman <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/09/20/cubs-third-baseman-alex-bregman-leaves-game-after-being-hit-in-face-by-foul-ball" >get hit with a foul ball Sunday</a> — and seeing <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/09/21/cubs-alex-bregman-foul-ball-face-injury-pictures" >the photos he posted</a> of the damage done to his face — it seemed like the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs" >Cubs</a> might be in for a nightmare scenario:</p><p>Being without their second best hitter as they attempt a deep playoff run.</p><p>But by Tuesday, the news on Bregman was relatively good.</p><p>The Cubs aren’t going to put their star third baseman, who suffered multiple facial fractures and is dealing with significant swelling in his face, on the injured list. It’s possible he could be back in action before the end of the regular season later this week.</p><p>“All things considered, we feel like he’s really lucky,” manager Craig Counsell said before Tuesday’s game. “He’s got multiple fractures in his left cheek area. None of them are to the point where the doctors deem surgery necessary or needed. And so he really is at a point where he can progress as tolerated.”</p><p>Bregman’s not dealing with nothing, as anyone who gets a look at him can tell.</p><p>But the guess was that things were going to be much, much worse for the Cubs.</p><p>Instead, they seem prepared to have Bregman at their disposal for the playoffs, which is why they inked him to a $175 million free-agent deal last offseason, bringing in <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/09/14/cubs-alex-bregman-career-playoff-games-postseason-world-series-braves-nl-wild-card-standings-mlb-playoff-matchups-carson-kelly-sprint-speed" >one of the most accomplished players in postseason history</a> to help them win a championship.</p><p>“Clearly, when everything was going down on Sunday afternoon, we all thought the worst-case [scenario] might be a possibility,” team president Jed Hoyer said, “and all the news since then has been really good.</p><p>“We have to take it one step at a time. We have to see how he’s doing when he’s moving around and active. But he’s in great spirits. … We just have to let him go through the steps a little bit here, but it’s been great news so far.”</p><p>What are those steps?</p><p>Bregman will continue to increase his workload from where it was Tuesday, when he did a light workout in the weight room and tracked pitches. Cubs brass pointed to the need for Bregman to start moving, taking ground balls and running – and do it all comfortably enough to get back in action.</p><p>But this is Bregman, lauded for his “relentless” work ethic. The Cubs expect nothing less than full dedication to make it back with critical games remaining.</p><p>“He doesn’t look great, that’s for sure,” Hoyer joked. “No one loves to play more than him. I can say that with no equivocation. I’ve never had a player that loves baseball as much as he does. He just wants to play all the time.</p><p>“Right away, when we first heard from him afterwards, [he said] he’s going to try to find a way to do it.”</p><p>The Cubs started the regular season’s final week tied atop the NL wild-card standings with the Padres and a game ahead of the Phillies, so there’s still a lot to play for in their last few games. They could land anywhere in those three wild-card spots, with four possible destinations for an opening-round, best-of-three series: Chicago, Philadelphia, San Diego and Atlanta.</p><p>Their preference is to play hosts at Wrigley Field, and Bregman would be helpful in attempting to secure that outcome. After MVP favorite Pete Crow-Armstrong, Bregman has been the team’s next best hitter, with an OPS north of 1.000 and nearly 20 homers in his last 61 games, while also playing Gold Glove caliber defense at third base.</p><p>The Cubs have faith in the fill-in ability of <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/09/17/cubs-pedro-ramirez-dansby-swanson-injury-shortstop-infield-outfield-free-agency" >reserve infielder Pedro Ramirez</a> – who started at third Tuesday – and utility man Matt Shaw, but a lineup without Bregman is one missing a key element.</p><p>But the vibe Tuesday was that any worries the Cubs would be operating at that deficit against playoff competition were unwarranted, with Bregman seemingly in the team’s October plans.</p><p>“I think Alex is going to be fine, I really do,” Counsell said. “The guy, he’s driving home from Cincinnati and he wants to play. He’s planning on playing.</p><p>“As long as symptoms don’t increase or happen as he increases activity, I think you’re going to see him play.”</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/09/21/cubs-alex-bregman-foul-ball-face-injury-pictures" >Cubs’ Alex Bregman shares photos after taking foul ball to face, reportedly has ‘multiple facial fractures’</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p></p>

entries.title: Downtown Chicago hotel workers vote to authorize strike
entries.summary: <p>Thousands of Chicago hotel workers could go on strike at any moment.</p><p>Members of Unite Here Local 1 voted Monday night to authorize a strike; its current contract expired Aug. 31.</p><p>“Tourism in Chicago is booming, all while inflation is increasing, and it’s affecting our hotel workers across the industry," Karen Kent, president of Unite Here Local 1, said in a statement issued by the union.</p><p>"They feel the weight anytime they go to the supermarket to buy food, or when they come home from work and are too tired to spend time with their family. Workers are ready to strike because they work too hard to live like this."</p><p>Local 1 represents attendants, cooks, dishwashers, front desk agents, servers and food service workers.</p><p>More than 85% of workers voted to go on strike in the first wave of voting, according to a union statement. The union has been negotiating since June with representatives of 46 hotels. Most are from three major hotel groups — Hyatt, Marriott and Hilton — though there are a few smaller operators. Most of the workers — about 7,000 — are downtown. </p><p>Based on a survey of its members, the union said about a third can’t cover rent or mortgage, while two-thirds had their hours cut during the slow period. Meanwhile, 1 in 4 workers took out payday or short-term loan to cover expenses.</p><p>According to Local 1, hotel operators Marriott, Hyatt and Hilton returned $22.3 billion to shareholders over the last three years.</p><p>On Tuesday, some union members were at East-West University in the Loop, where they could sign up for benefits available from the union if workers decide to strike.</p><div always the hope. entries.title: Finance Committee backs $201.6M subsidy for Foundry Park mega-project
entries.summary: <p>Foundry Park, a developer’s $3 billion replacement for the failed Lincoln Yards mega-project on the North Side, moved closer to reality Tuesday over the objections of a powerful union.</p><p>The City Council’s Finance Committee signed off on Mayor Brandon Johnson’s plan for a <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/city-hall/2026/07/15/megaprojects-tifs-the-78-foundry-park-projects" >$201.6 million tax increment financing (TIF) subsidy</a> that would pave the way for JDL Development to start construction of Phase One of the scaled-down project “before the end of the year.”</p><p>It passed by voice vote, without a roll call.</p><p>Before the vote, representatives for Unite Here Local 1 urged the Finance Committee to withhold the city subsidy until there’s a guarantee of union jobs at a 200,000 square foot hotel planned for the site.</p><p>Foundry Park developer Jim Letchinger told the Finance Committee he's a “strong believer in Chicago unions” and has had conversations with Unite Here. But, Letchinger said he “can’t make any commitments” because he is not a hotel operator and hasn’t chosen one yet.</p><p>“Once we get it financed, discussions can take place,” Letchinger said.</p><p>Downtown Ald. Brendan Reilly (42nd) told the developer: “This is a union town. It is very important to myself and others that we do right by folks who work in these properties.”</p><p>Letchinger said he has “zero doubt” about his ability to deliver “everything that I’ve promised" with the help of the subsidy.</p><p>“We are promising to build parks, to build a riverwalk, to improve the existing roadwork. We have a pedestrian and bike bridge to connect the 606 if and when it arrives at our site. That’s what we’ve committed to do. That’s what we’re going to do,” Letchinger told the Sun-Times Tuesday.</p><p>“The more we build, the more money will be available for other [infrastructure] projects. If we don’t start building anything, there’s no money.”</p><p>In 2018, then-Mayor Rahm Emanuel proposed a $1.3 billion subsidy for the North Side mega-project known as <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/real-estate/2025/06/27/lincoln-yards-sterling-bay-jdl-development-jim-letchinger-rahm-emanuel" >Lincoln Yards </a>that became a political lightning rod for the Chicago Teachers Union, and a symbol of Emanuel’s pro-business priorities.</p><p>The massive subsidy pledge was not enough to save Lincoln Yards. The mega-project on prime industrial land along the Chicago River collapsed under pressure from rising interest rates and slow demand exacerbated by the pandemic.</p><p>The $201.6 million TIF subsidy approved Tuesday pales by comparison to the assistance Emanuel promised to Lincoln Yards. It will support just over 25% of the $800 million worth of roads, bridges, utilities and mass transit improvements Ald. Brian Hopkins (2nd) has said were mandated as part of the Lincoln Yards plan.</p><p>Hopkins helped muscle the Lincoln Yards subsidy through the City Council before losing the project to Ald. Scott Waguespack (32nd) in the new ward map.</p><p>Letchinger has acknowledged there is “other infrastructure that the neighborhood would like to see done that is not possible right now.” That includes another bridge crossing over the Chicago River and a realignment of Elston Avenue, which Letchinger called a “massive undertaking” complicated by cost and property control that no private developer can accomplish.</p><p>The same goes for the 606 extension, which is “up to the county and the city,” the developer said.</p><p>“If they are able to extend it to our property, we will then take it across the river and continue it in front of our property. But they have to get it over to us first,” Letchinger said.</p><p>Waguespack said much of the reduced subsidy will be used to redesign and rebuild local streets like Southport and Cortland that, for decades, were closed to accommodate companies like Finkl Steel.</p><p>“There were no modern sewer systems. There were no modern roads. So we have to reopen everything, rebuild everything, put in lighting and remove a lot of rail,” Waguespack said. “The public gets streets and roads that are actually passable. If you go through there now, it’s all ground-down rail and you can’t really get through there without almost like a four-wheel drive" vehicle.</p><p>There will be “at least half a dozen pocket parks” and walkways that Waguespack said will pave the way for "the whole riverfront to become a 60-foot riverfront setback. </p><p>“In the Lincoln Yards plan, they kept it at 30 feet” of riverfront space, he said. “We doubled it so there are kayak launches and areas where people can relax along the river."</p><p>Letchinger’s plan for roughly 34 vacant acres of the site calls for up to 3,737 residences, 20% of them designated as affordable to comply with the city’s set-aside rules.</p><p>The new design includes low- to mid-rise buildings, some for offices, grouped near open space and riverfront access. Buildings would get ground-floor retail, and one is slated as a boutique hotel.</p><p>Waguespack embraced the project’s lower density and dramatically reduced subsidy.</p><p>“This will get the project built, and it’s not focused on mega-projects that I don’t think many believed would come to fruition,” Waguespack said.</p><p>Lincoln Yards developer Sterling Bay “wanted a massive Elston-Armitage intersection with a new bridge over Ashland Avenue,” but Waguespack said “a lot of what they were saying with the new Metra station was never going to come to fruition. The TIF would have never been able to pay for it.”</p><p>Waguespack said the $201.6 million subsidy will cover "basic infrastructure" and "no private costs."</p><p>“Under the Sterling Bay deal, they could get reimbursed for all of their legal costs and marketing and they wanted that money in the millions. That’s not happening in this," he said.</p>

entries.title: Colorado player apologizes for remarks demeaning Northwestern's temporary football stadium
entries.summary: <p>BOULDER, Colo. — Colorado defensive back Ben Finneseth spoke to reporters before coach Deion Sanders' news conference and apologized after he was caught in a video speaking harshly of Northwestern's temporary stadium before Saturday's game, a 41-7 NU victory. A player in a video posted on social media can be heard saying, "(expletive) sounds like a (expletive) library. It's football."</p><p>Finneseth said Tuesday: "It was childish. It was a stupid thing that I said. It won't happen again, and the way I handled it was horrible. I promise you guys that it will not happen again, and it will be much more mature moving forward. So I apologize."</p><p>Before Finneseth left, Sanders shook his hand and added, "that's why I love you."</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/college-sports/2026/09/19/aidan-chiles-and-joseph-himon-lead-northwestern-to-rout-of-visiting-colorado" >Aidan Chiles and Joseph Himon lead Northwestern to rout of visiting Colorado</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p>Sanders then announced he had dismissed several players from the team.</p><p>The Buffaloes coach didn't specify Tuesday which players were no longer with the program but indicated it was for a pattern of behavior and not just what transpired in the loss to the Wildcats in Evanston. </p><p>"It's never one thing," Sanders said. "Those guys will tell you: I'm the most loving, giving and forgiving man you can ever meet. But when you start being conduct detrimental to the team that will set us back in things that you're doing — you don't care about the team. You care about you. I have a problem with that."</p><p>Sanders referenced last season when things went sideways and the team finished 3-9.</p><p>"A year ago, I didn't put my foot down in it enough," he said. "It lingered a little bit. Then, it imploded. I'm not doing that. I'm not doing that anymore."</p><p>Sanders expressed his frustration Saturday night and acknowledged that he got on a few players for their reaction after the loss. He said: "I don't understand how you can have joy in a loss, especially when I'm upset and I'm walking right behind you."</p><p>The coach took accountability, too.</p><p>"I don't push the buck and push the blame on anyone else. It's on me," Sanders said Tuesday. "We want to win the right way, and we want to do what's right. But the whole thing is about winning. We don't want to ever employ a losing type of sentiment. We don't want to do things that are associated with losers and bad-mouth opponents and do that kind of stuff. That's not who we are."</p><p>The Buffaloes (2-1) are trying to rebound after a game in which they had four turnovers and committed nine penalties for 80 yards.</p><p>"A loss by 10, a loss by three, a loss by 30 — it hurts me. There's no degrees of loss," Sanders said. "Like, there's no degrees of sin. A sin is a sin. A loss is a loss to me."</p><p>Sanders is putting everything under a microscope as the Buffaloes prepare for Saturday's game at Baylor. At the top of the list: penalties.</p><p>Colorado has 28 penalties for 247 yards so far this season. It's frustrating to Sanders, who pointed out the team is disciplined in everything it does on the practice field.</p><p>"Then when you get out from the field and you're undisciplined, I don't understand," Sanders said. "It's hard to fathom.</p><p>"We're challenging them to be who they say they want to be."</p><p>The message hit home for players such as linebacker Tyler Martinez, who recently received a "D" patch — it stands for "Dawg" — from the coaching staff for being a playmaker.</p><p>"It's hard to see somebody go," Martinez said of the dismissals. "Like Coach Prime said, it's about the team. If you're about yourself, got to do what's best for us."</p><p>Sanders had several leaders approach him about how to get ahead of this so more dismissals don't occur. They want to help stay on top of the situation.</p><p>"I applaud them for that," Sanders said, "coming to me ready to get ahead of it."<br></p>

entries.title: Donda West Way: A South Shore street is renamed for a Chicago 'village mom'
entries.summary: <p>A group of Chicago-bred hip-hop legends gathered for a South Shore reunion, and for a moment, they transported to their teenage years — making music in the living room of their chosen mom, Donda West.</p><p>“This is not just a story about Donda West's son,” said Chicago Public Schools Board member and rapper Che “Rhymefest” Smith. “This is really a story about a woman who raised a community of boys.”</p><p>West was known for being the mother of hip-hop artist Ye, formerly known as Kanye West. To many Chicagoans, she was also an English professor, a former Chicago State University department chairperson, a businesswoman, a Fulbright scholar — and as Smith would call it, a “village mom.”</p><p>The two-story blue house on the city’s South Side was both the Wests’ home and where Ye’s music career was launched alongside his childhood friends. Now signs on 78th Street between South Shore Drive and Coles Avenue, at two nearby intersections, bear Donda West’s name.</p><p>“I love my biological mama, and I'm so proud to have a village mom like Dr. Donda West,” Smith said, with the crowd erupting in cheers.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" entries.title: Great Lakes senators call on Trump to stop delaying invasive carp barrier
entries.summary: <p>Great Lakes Democratic lawmakers — including Illinois Sens. Dick Durbin and Tammy Duckworth — are warning the Trump administration that any more delays to a $1.15 billion barrier project to keep invasive carp out of Lake Michigan could put the economy of the region at risk.</p><p>Five senators from Illinois, Michigan, and Wisconsin are calling for a meeting to discuss the repeated pauses around the Brandon Road Interbasin Project and “steps the administration will take to ensure the project is completed as quickly as possible,” according to a new <a class="Link" href="https://www.documentcloud.org/documents/28672017-brandon-road-work-stoppage-letter-to-army-corps/" target="_blank" >letter </a>addressed to D. Lee Forsgren, acting assistant secretary of the Army for Civil Works.</p><p>“We urge the Administration to ensure the Brandon Road Interbasin Project moves forward without further interruption,” the letter states. “We also urge consistent and transparent communication with the non-federal sponsors in the future in advance of any changes to the project.”</p><p>Michigan Sens. Elissa Slotkin and Gary Peters and Wisconsin Sen. Tammy Baldwin also signed the letter.</p><p>The letter comes after President Donald Trump and the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers placed the megaproject near suburban Joliet under administrative review, halting work at the site for the second time in less than a year. While that most recent stop-work order was lifted this month, legislators wrote that the delays are increasing the already hefty price tag of the project. Illinois and Michigan are contributing $50 million and $64 million respectively.</p><p>The megaproject is anchored on the Brandon Road Lock and Dam, a choke point on the Des Plaines River where the Army Corps wants to lodge a multilayered underwater defense system boasting sonic blasts, bubble walls, an electric barrier and an updated flushing mechanism.</p><p>Lawmakers and policy experts worry that the delays risk extending the decadelong timeline, potentially increasing the chances that the invasive carp make into the Great Lakes.</p><p>These concerns were amplified this summer by the discovery that hundreds of juvenile invasive carp found just 80 miles downstream from Lake Michigan, the farthest north the young fish have been found since the state began monitoring in 2010.</p><p>Adult carp have been routinely seen as close as 50 miles away from Lake Michigan near the confluence of the Kankakee and Des Plaines rivers and headwaters of the Illinois River.</p><p>The invasive carp — the silver carp and the bighead carp in particular — are a voracious family of fish that can outeat and outgrow native species. The decades-long concern among scientists and policy experts is that if the nuisance fish make it past the Illinois River and into Lake Michigan, it could upend the largest freshwater ecosystem on the planet and the multibillion recreational and fishing industries that depend on it.</p><p>The Brandon Road Interbasin Project was first presented as a solution to the advancing front on invasive fish back in 2014. Congress authorized the project six years later, and then provided an initial $225 million for the first state of construction with an additional $47 million in 2023, and $28 million in 2026. Crews began work on the project last spring before it was paused just a couple months later.</p><p>“Invasive carp are a serious threat to our Great Lakes, and the Brandon Road Interbasin Project is our best defense against the irreparable harm these fish could do to our lakes’ ecosystem,” Durbin said in a statement to WBEZ. </p><p>“Time is of the essence as these carp are inching closer to Lake Michigan, and we do not have time for the Trump Administration to interfere with the project by arbitrarily pausing the project without explanation.”</p>
