entries.title: First hockey, now baseball: FutureSports deal with MLB will let fans bet on teams
entries.summary: <p>Chicago startup FutureSports is expanding the opportunity for traders and fans to take monetary positions on sports, in a new deal with MLB.</p><p>FutureSports said Monday it will establish financial indexes based on the performance of the Cubs, White Sox and 28 other teams in the league using in-game statistics provided by MLB. The futures contracts will be offered by Loop-based CME Group, which operates the world’s largest derivatives exchange.</p><p>“Our mission is to evolve sports or transition sports out of the binary, sort of, entertainment realm and into the institutional risk management sector,” FutureSports co-founder Rhett Dinsdale said.</p><p>Binary options are mostly affiliated with prediction markets, like <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/politics/2026/06/25/kalshi-lawsuit-illinois-tax-pritzker-prediction-markets" >Kalshi</a> and Polymarket, which offer yes-or-no wagers tied to real world outcomes.</p><p>Futures contracts, by contrast, focus on asset price changes over time, allowing savvy everyday and institutional traders to hedge against price swings — commonly associated with financial and agricultural products — or speculate on price movements.</p><p>The deal comes about a month after FutureSports announced a similar <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/money/2026/08/15/chicago-startups-futuresports-cme-nhl-etf-bet-sports" >landmark agreement with the NHL</a>, following a partnership with CME to help launch the indexes. Futures indexes and contracts tied to NHL teams are scheduled to launch Sept. 28, the day before the season opener.</p><p>Even though baseball is in its last week of games — with the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs" >Cubs</a> and <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox" >White Sox</a> vying for rare playoff berths in the same year — Dinsdale inferred regulatory approvals could be on deck. </p><p>“I wouldn't rule anything out,” he said.</p><h3>Inside baseball</h3><p>Dinsdale and FutureSports co-founder Leigh Taylforth have been courting MLB since 2022, when they started the company in Australia before relocating to Chicago.</p><p>A pair of its influential investors played key roles in introducing the duo to MLB decision-makers and during negotiations, according to Dinsdale.</p><p>“Elysian Park and John Henry and his family office have been instrumental in helping us secure a deal at the MLB,” he said. “It’s been a long hard road, but we're there. And we think we've got an excellent partner in MLB, and we’re excited to get some products out there.”</p><p>Elysian Park Ventures is the investment arm of the Los Angeles Dodgers' ownership group. Henry, a legendary investment manager and commodities trader, founded Fenway Sports Group, which owns the Boston Red Sox, Liverpool Football Club, Pittsburgh Penguins and other sports assets.</p><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Pat Nabong/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Other FutureSports financial backers include Cubs ownership group Marquee Ventures, trading platform Robinhood and CME.</p><p>The MLB index, similar to the NHL index, will open at 7,500 points and fluctuate throughout a game based on real-time statistical data, as well as in-game, seasonal and championship milestones, according to FutureSports.</p><p>MLB is not involved in the determination, calculation or governance of indexes. And like the NHL, MLB players, coaches, umpires and staff are prohibited from trading CME FutureSports Performance Indexes baseball futures contracts, the league confirmed. </p><p>Fenway Sports Group and the White Sox declined to comment. Elysian Park and the Cubs didn't respond to a request for comment.</p><h3>Confluence of factors</h3><p>The latest play by FutureSports and CME aims to capture more retail traders while tapping into the global sports industry, which the firm Research and Markets pegs to hit $651 billion in sales in 2028.</p><p>“We believe there is an opportunity to bring investing and hedging discipline to the business of professional baseball,” Tim McCourt, CME’s senior managing director and global head of equities, FX and alternative products, said.</p><p>Retail trading has exploded the last few years amid the popularity of trading apps like Robinhood, investor chat rooms on Reddit and the booming business of prediction markets and their proliferation in everyday life, from in-game advertisements to social media campaigns.</p><p>Trading volume on eight of the leading prediction market platforms on Sept. 13, the first Sunday of NFL games, topped $3.1 billion, nearly surpassing the record from the previous day of college football games, according to a Jeffries analyst note cited by Front Office Sports.</p><p>“There is no doubt that sports prediction markets have definitely helped open up the markets' eyes to the possibility of sports as an asset class,” Dinsdale said.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/money/2026/08/15/chicago-startups-futuresports-cme-nhl-etf-bet-sports" >Chicago startup’s NHL deal creates new way to bet on sports teams’ performance</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p></p>

entries.title: Comienza la limpieza en Douglass Park después del pantano que dejó la lluvia durante Riot Fest
entries.summary: <p>Se acabó el Riot Fest 2026. Pero en Douglass Park queda un recuerdo: mucho lodo, después de que las fuertes lluvias del fin de semana convirtieran el terreno en un pantano al cierre del último espectáculo.</p><p>Un grupo comunitario, Únete La Villita, <a class="Link" href="https://www.instagram.com/reels/Ddjo1-txkDV/" target="_blank" >publicó en Instagram</a> el lunes que el parque está “completamente destruido” y añadió preocupaciones sobre los “efectos a largo plazo del festival que ‘solo dura tres días’”, además de señalar que documentarán la restauración durante el próximo año.</p><p>El fundador de Riot Fest, Mike Petryshyn, dijo en un comunicado el lunes por la tarde que la “responsabilidad de su equipo no termina cuando acaba el festival. Estamos comprometidos a restaurar el parque, trabajando junto con el Distrito de Parques y la comunidad, y a darle seguimiento a ese trabajo”.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>El domingo, los asistentes tuvieron dificultades para cruzar los campos lodosos de Douglass Park, y algunos perdieron sus zapatos en el lodo.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Ashlee Rezin/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Un fin de semana de lluvia continua y el intenso flujo de personas, con unos 50,000 asistentes diarios estimados, dificultó moverse por el parque el domingo por la tarde, cuando subieron al escenario los actos más esperados, entre ellos Alanis Morissette y William Shatner.</p><p>Cuando los fanáticos finalmente se iban, algunos perdieron los zapatos en el lodo, mientras otros quedaron atascados y fueron ayudados por desconocidos en un esfuerzo colectivo por avanzar por el pantano.</p><p>Ahora gran parte de la atención se centra en cómo lucirán las reparaciones de Douglass Park en los próximos días. El cronograma para restaurar y reabrir por completo el parque ya fue modificado.</p><p>Antes y después del evento de tres días, los organizadores de Riot Fest reciben tiempo para montar y luego desmontar el sitio. En el <a class="Link" href="https://riotfest.org/park-impact/#access" target="_blank" >sitio web de Riot Fest,</a> el cronograma de 2026 había fijado del 21 al 24 de septiembre para la salida de producción, limpieza y restauración. El 25 de septiembre figuraba como la fecha en que el parque estaría totalmente abierto al público.</p><p>Pero la salida de producción ahora se aplazó hasta el 29 de septiembre, “si el clima y las condiciones del terreno lo permiten”, según los organizadores. “Inmediatamente después de la salida de producción, Riot Fest, su equipo de restauración y el Distrito de Parques de Chicago evaluarán las áreas afectadas y comenzarán a implementar el plan de restauración”, dijeron los organizadores en un comunicado.</p><p>Hasta el momento de publicación, la oficina de la concejal Monique Scott (24.°) no había respondido a una solicitud de comentarios sobre el cronograma proyectado, qué incluirán las reparaciones ni cuánto podrían costar.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Los asistentes a Riot Fest empujan una carreola por el lodo profundo mientras llueve en Douglass Park durante el tercer día.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Ashlee Rezin/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Los fanáticos tuvieron opiniones encontradas sobre el desastre.</p><p>“Mientras caminen un pie delante del otro, todo va a estar bien… Es punk rock, es Riot Fest. Todos la están pasando bien”, dijo Alex Ramos, de Rogers Park, un asistente habitual que acudió el domingo para ver a Pierce the Veil y Pennywise. “Hemos seguido viendo a todos [los artistas], pero peleando con los elementos, como se pueden imaginar”.</p><p>Joe Theis, de 52 años, que viajó desde Denver, coincidió en que los asistentes parecían tomar el lodo con calma.</p><p>“Nunca llegué a Woodstock ‘99, con la gente del lodo y todo eso, pero esto es lo más cerca que he estado”, dijo. “Parece que todos están lidiando más o menos bien”.</p><p>Grace Elliott, de 35 años, de Cleveland, usa un andador y describió las dificultades para moverse por el parque a medida que empeoraban las condiciones.</p><p>“Las ruedas... se estaban atascando con el lodo y el pasto, e incluso al pasar por las astillas de madera, era más como arrastrar mi ayuda de movilidad, y... mis pies se quedaron pegados al suelo”.</p><p>Elliott visitó una carpa de accesibilidad en el lugar y calificó al personal allí de “muy empático”, aunque dijo que se quedó sin opciones y al final decidió irse.</p><p>“No nos dijeron directamente que teníamos que irnos a casa, pero realmente no había opciones para mucha gente, especialmente para personas como yo que usamos un dispositivo de movilidad”, agregó, y sugirió para el futuro más rampas y senderos de metal, así como el uso de carritos de golf o vehículos todoterreno para ayudar a las personas con movilidad limitada a moverse por el parque en caso de mal clima.</p><p>El <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/entertainment-and-culture/2025/04/10/3-year-riot-fest-deal-draws-mixed-reviews-from-residents-around-douglass-park" target="_blank" >contrato actual de tres años</a> de Riot Fest en Douglass Park se extiende hasta 2027. Lauren Quinn, subdirectora de ingresos del Distrito de Parques de Chicago, dijo que el departamento generará entre $3 millones y $4.5 millones gracias al acuerdo mediante tarifas anuales de permiso.</p><p>En 2026, el acuerdo exige que los organizadores de Riot Fest paguen $5.375 por boleto. Para 2027, sube a $5.50 por boleto, con una estimación de 150,000 boletos vendidos en los tres días.</p><p>Del dinero recaudado, el Distrito de Parques tiene una política de “retribución” del 30% específicamente para Douglass Park, lo que significa que entre $900,000 y $1.2 millones se destinan exclusivamente a mejoras en el terreno del vecindario de North Lawndale. El contrato también establece que Riot Fest aportará un 10% adicional para “mejoras de capital en Douglass Park”.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" entries.title: OEMC begins rollout of new 911 dispatch system despite concerns from City Council members
entries.summary: <p>The city of Chicago began rolling out a new 911 dispatch system Tuesday that officials say will help improve emergency response times.</p><p>The new computer-aided dispatch system went live, despite pushback from aldermen who urged Mayor Brandon Johnson’s office to slow the implementation until they received assurances that the system was ready.</p><p>In a letter sent to the mayor last week, 14 aldermen expressed concerns and requested additional information, saying significant questions about the system remain unanswered.</p><p>“We support modernization, but it cannot come at the expense of the safety of Chicago residents or the police officers, firefighters, paramedics, call takers and dispatchers who depend on this system,” the letter said. “Public reporting has raised concerns about system stability, new workflows, call handling and callback functionality, delayed information, and the adequacy of hands-on training.”</p><p>Ald. Chris Taliaferro (29th) said City Council members brought their concerns to the mayor's office when they heard from OEMC employees and dispatchers that the new system was dropping calls and some calls were not routed to the correct department. </p><p>But in a response letter, the mayor’s office said the system has undergone extensive stress testing, including a test in which it handled 3,800 911 calls — or 150% of the city’s busiest call hours — in a single hour and “met the response-time requirements specified in the contract.”</p><p>The city signed a nearly $75 million contract with provider CentralSquare Technologies in 2019 to upgrade the 30-year-old system it had been using. </p><p>Officials said the new system will improve emergency response times by up to 33 seconds and that it will streamline police, fire and emergency medical dispatch operations by providing a common platform that allows all departments to access the same information in real time.</p><p>For now, the new system will operate alongside the older system “in order to maintain and ensure Chicago’s public safety infrastructure,” Johnson’s office said Tuesday.</p><p>Taliaferro said he appreciated Johnson's “quick response” to the concerns and called the decision to keep the legacy system in place as a backup the “right move.”</p><p>"It gives us an opportunity to look at this a little further to see if we do have a functional system," he said. "And if some of the concerns that were expressed to us doesn't rise to the need to cease operation of the new CAD system."</p><p>The mayor’s office said there is no specific date for when the new system will fully take over, allowing officials to make adjustments and address any contingencies that may arise during the transition. </p><p>However, the office said the “process would be completed this fall.”</p><p>Dispatchers began training to use the new system in October 2025 and have completed more than 4,600 hours of classroom instruction, city officials said.</p><p>Taliaferro, who serves on the Committee on Public Safety, said the group will follow up with the mayor’s office and OEMC next month to check on the system’s progress.</p><p>Johnson’s office said it will begin offering briefings with aldermen next week.</p>
